title: Gone from sight: how dirty water hides, travels and builds up

summary.text: Five drops of colour turn a tumbler of water bright. Pour one spoonful into fresh water, and again, and again, and the colour fades until your eyes cannot find it. Is it gone? Your nose may say no. In this unit you thin out colour and scent step by step and test your eyes against your nose. Then you follow dirty water further. You see how oil spreads and how hard it is to clear, how a little pollution piles up inside fish and the animals that eat them, and how a sewage plant uses living microbes to clean water. You also find out why 'clean' always depends on what is being checked, and by whom.
summary.art: Five clear tumblers in a row on white paper, the first bright red, the next two fading to pink, the last two looking like plain water, with a small teaspoon between each pair.

intro.hook: Two tumblers of water stand side by side. Both look exactly like water from the tap. Into one of them, someone stirred a spoonful of kewra essence. Can you tell which one, without tasting?
intro.text: Look as hard as you like, and the two look the same. Now bring each tumbler to your nose. One smells of flowers and the other of nothing. Your eyes could not find the difference, but your nose could. So when a river, a pond or a well 'looks clear', what has been checked, and what has not?
intro.art: Two identical clear tumblers on a kitchen counter, a small bottle of kewra essence and a teaspoon beside them, and a child leaning in to sniff one tumbler.

outcomes: I can explain that thinning dirty water out spreads the dirt through more water, but the amount of dirt stays the same.
I can name the main kinds of water pollution (bits that float or sink, dissolved things, living things, extra plant food) and say which tool can take out which.
I can run a blind test with a fair control, write down the results, and say how likely they were by chance alone.
I can explain how waste that microbes can eat uses up the oxygen that fish breathe.
I can explain how a pollutant that bodies cannot break down builds up along a food chain.
I can describe the stages of a sewage treatment plant and say what each stage takes out.
I can explain why 'clean water' depends on what is checked and who or what checks it, and why measuring beats looking.

terms.meaning: Mixing something into more water so that it is spread thinner. The same amount is there, but it is weaker.
terms.example: One spoon of coloured water stirred into a full tumbler of clear water.
terms.art: A teaspoon of red liquid going into a tumbler of clear water, with the red spreading out into pale pink.

terms.meaning: How much of a substance is in a certain amount of water. A strong mix has a high concentration. A thin mix has a low one.
terms.example: Sweet tea has a higher concentration of sugar than tea with one pinch.
terms.art: Two tumblers, one dark red and one pale pink, with a label above each saying strong and weak.

terms.meaning: A way to write a very small concentration. One part per million means one tiny part in every million parts of water.
terms.example: One drop of colour in a full bathtub of water is less than one part per million.
terms.art: A bathtub of clear water with a single red drop falling into it, and a magnified circle showing one red dot among a million clear dots.

terms.meaning: Used water from toilets, bathrooms and kitchens, with the waste it carries.
terms.example: The water that goes down the drain of a flat goes into a sewer pipe.
terms.art: A cut-away of a city street showing a house drain joining a large underground sewer pipe.

terms.meaning: Liquid waste that flows out of a factory, a farm or a treatment plant.
terms.example: The water that a dyeing factory lets out after washing cloth.
terms.art: A pipe from a factory wall pouring coloured water into a drain.

terms.meaning: Rain water that runs over the ground and carries things with it into drains, streams and lakes.
terms.example: After a storm, rain washes oil and dust from a road into the drain.
terms.art: Rain falling on a road, with brown streams running to a drain, carrying leaves, plastic and a rainbow sheen of oil.

terms.meaning: A substance that living things use as food to grow. Too much of it in water can be a problem.
terms.example: The nitrogen in fertiliser feeds crops, and also feeds algae in a pond.
terms.art: A hand sprinkling fertiliser on a paddy field, with a stream carrying some of it toward a pond.

terms.meaning: A sudden crowd of algae that turns the water green and thick. It happens when the water has a lot of nutrients.
terms.example: A pond covered in green scum in the summer.
terms.art: A pond covered in a bright green mat of algae, with a few fish looking up from below the surface.

terms.meaning: Oxygen gas mixed into water, in tiny bubbles too small to see. Fish and many other water animals breathe it through their gills.
terms.example: A cold glass of water grows bubbles as it warms, because dissolved air comes out.
terms.art: A fish with open gills, with tiny oxygen bubbles drawn in the water around it.

terms.meaning: Able to be eaten and broken down by microbes into simple things that soil and water can use.
terms.example: A banana peel rots in a few weeks, but a plastic cover stays for many years.
terms.art: A banana peel half rotted into soil on one side, and a plastic cover lying whole beside it.

terms.meaning: A substance building up inside a living body, because the body takes it in faster than it can get rid of it.
terms.example: Mercury builds up in the body of a big fish over her whole life.
terms.art: A tiny fish, a bigger fish and a heron in a row, each with a bigger pile of black dots drawn inside its body.

terms.meaning: A place that cleans used water before it goes back to a river or a lake, or is used again.
terms.example: Many large apartment blocks have a small plant in the basement or at the back.
terms.art: A cut-away of a treatment plant with four tanks in a row, water getting clearer from left to right.

terms.meaning: A living being whose presence tells you how clean the water is, because they can live only in clean water, or only in dirty water.
terms.example: Mayfly nymphs live in clean streams. Red sludge worms live in very dirty ones.
terms.art: Two small drawings side by side: a mayfly nymph on a clean stone, and a bunch of red sludge worms in dark mud.

terms.meaning: How cloudy water is, because of tiny bits floating in it.
terms.example: Water after rain in a river is muddy and has high turbidity.
terms.art: Three tumblers in a row: clear water, slightly cloudy water and thick muddy water.

terms.meaning: A thin layer of oil floating on the surface of water.
terms.example: A rainbow shine on a puddle in a car park.
terms.art: A puddle in a car park with a rainbow-coloured film of oil on the surface.

explanations.concept: Dirty water: bits, dissolved things and living things
explanations.definition: Water pollution is anything added to water that harms the living beings who use it. It comes in three main kinds. Some are bits that float or sink, some are dissolved, and some are living, such as germs.
explanations.description: Bits are things you can pick out: plastic, leaves, mud and oil. They float on top or sink to the bottom. Dissolved things have spread out into single tiny pieces, so they cannot be seen or caught. Salt, sugar, dye and many chemicals are like this. Living pollution means germs from sewage, such as the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid. Each kind needs a different way to clean it. A net takes out floating bits. A cloth takes out mud. Neither can take out salt.
examples: A plastic bag floating in a lake is a bit that floats. A net can lift it out.
Mud in a monsoon river is a bit that sinks. If you leave the water still, it settles.
Detergent in a drain is dissolved. A cloth cannot catch it.
Germs from sewage are living. Chlorine or boiling kills them.
explanations.art: Three tumblers in a row: one with a floating plastic bag, one with mud settling at the bottom, and one clear with a few dots labelled dissolved, beside a tiny drawing of germs.

explanations.concept: Where dirty water comes from: one pipe or the whole land
explanations.definition: A point source is one place where pollution enters, such as a drain pipe. Runoff is pollution that arrives from the whole land at once, carried by rain.
explanations.description: A point source is easy to find and to stop. You can walk to the pipe and put a filter on it. Runoff is much harder. Rain washes oil from roads, fertiliser from fields, litter from streets and soil from building sites into drains. In India, the biggest single source of river pollution is sewage. The Central Pollution Control Board reports that less than half of the sewage made in Indian towns and cities is treated, and the rest flows on to rivers and lakes. Industry, farms and festivals add more.
examples: A factory pipe pouring dyed water into a stream is a point source.
Rain washing fertiliser from many fields into a river is runoff.
Thousands of idols dipped in a lake after a festival add paint and clay to the water at one time of year.
explanations.art: A river seen from above, with one pipe from a factory on one bank, and many thin brown streams of runoff from fields and roads on the other bank.

explanations.concept: Dilution: the amount stays, the strength falls
explanations.definition: Dilution means spreading a substance through more water. The concentration, which is the strength, goes down. The amount does not.
explanations.description: Stir one spoonful of coloured water into a tumbler of clear water. The mix has a pale colour. Take one spoonful of that and stir it into another clear tumbler, and the colour fades again. After a few steps your eyes see nothing. But the colour was never destroyed. Atoms and molecules are not used up when they mix. Each spoonful carries a little of the colour, and the rest stays behind in the earlier tumblers. Your nose usually keeps finding a scent for longer than your eyes keep finding a colour, but it gives out in the end too. Scientists write tiny strengths as parts per million.
examples: A spoonful of coloured water stirred into a tumbler of clear water makes a mix 41 times weaker than the spoonful.
One drop of ink in a bucket vanishes to the eye, but a chemist's instrument can still find it.
A chemist's instrument can find some chemicals at less than one part in a billion.
explanations.art: A row of four tumblers, each one paler than the one before, with arrows showing one spoonful going from each tumbler into the next.

explanations.concept: Is the sea big enough to take our waste?
explanations.description: For a long time, engineers said, 'The solution to pollution is dilution.' A river or the sea is huge, so waste poured in would thin out to nothing. Some of this is true. Small amounts of natural waste, such as leaves, are broken down by microbes in a river. But many things are not broken down, and they do not thin out to nothing. They are carried far away, they settle in mud, and they build up in living bodies. Scientists today still use dilution in planning, but they set strict limits on what can be let out.
examples: A small amount of kitchen waste in a fast, clean river is eaten by microbes within days.
Mercury poured into Minamata Bay in Japan did not thin out to nothing. It built up in fish and then in people.
Plastic waste thrown into rivers in one country is found on beaches far away.

perspectives.explanation: Rivers and seas are so large that waste put into them is thinned to harmless levels. Cities can pour sewage and factory waste into them.
Thinning lowers the strength, but not the amount. Many pollutants do not break down, settle in mud and build up in animals. Waste must be treated before it is let out.
Mixing is still part of safe design. A treated stream is let into a river at a rate that the river can mix and clean. The key is to measure, and not to guess from how the water looks.

explanations.art: A big river seen from above with a thin line of brown water from a pipe mixing into the blue, and downstream a fish with dark dots in the body.

explanations.concept: Dissolved things: too small for any cloth
explanations.definition: Dissolved means spread out into single atoms, ions or molecules, so small that no cloth or sand can catch them.
explanations.description: A grain of mud is made of billions of atoms and can be seen with a magnifying glass. When salt dissolves, the salt breaks into single ions. An ion is an atom, or a small group of atoms, with an electric charge. Water holds each one apart. A single ion is thousands of times narrower than a grain of fine mud. A filter has gaps that are far too big to stop it. That is why sand and cloth clean muddy water but leave salty water as salty. Cleaning dissolved pollution needs other methods, such as charcoal that holds chemicals on its surface, or reverse osmosis, which pushes water through a skin with the tiniest holes.
examples: Salty water poured through a cloth stays salty.
Charcoal in a water filter takes out some dissolved chemicals and smells.
A reverse osmosis purifier removes most dissolved salts, but also wastes a lot of water.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drawing of a cloth with gaps, mud grains stuck on top, and tiny dots labelled ions passing through the gaps with the water.

explanations.concept: Food in the water uses up the oxygen
explanations.definition: When waste that microbes can eat gets into water, the microbes multiply and use up the dissolved oxygen. Fish and other animals can then no longer breathe.
explanations.description: Kitchen waste, sewage and dead plants are food for microbes. When a lot of food reaches a pond, bacteria multiply and eat the food. They breathe the oxygen dissolved in the water as they do. Fresh oxygen from the air mixes in only slowly. If the bacteria use oxygen faster than fresh oxygen arrives, the water runs short. Fish crowd to the surface, gasp, and then die. So the harm is not poison. It is that the waste fed a huge crowd of microbes, and they all breathe. Scientists measure this as BOD, the oxygen the microbes need to eat the waste.
examples: Fish floating dead in a lake the morning after a heavy sewage flow.
A pond where leaves from many trees pile up in summer, and the fish come to the top at dawn.
A scientist's meter that shows 2 milligrams of oxygen in a litre, too low for most fish.
explanations.art: A pond at dawn with fish gasping at the surface, and a magnified circle showing bacteria crowding around floating waste, each with a small bubble of oxygen being pulled in.

explanations.concept: Too much plant food: algal blooms
explanations.definition: Nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae. When too much reaches a lake, the algae grow into a thick green crowd called an algal bloom.
explanations.description: Fertiliser, detergent and sewage all carry nitrogen and phosphorus. These are the same foods that make crops grow. In a lake they make algae grow too. The algae cover the surface and block the sunlight from plants below. When the algae die, microbes eat them, and use up the oxygen, as in the last card. So a lake can turn green first and then run short of oxygen. Some blooms also make poisons. In Bengaluru, lakes such as Bellandur have been covered with white foam and floating weed, which people link to detergents and sewage.
examples: A farm pond that turns green a week after fertiliser is spread nearby.
Foam on a polluted lake, made partly of detergent.
Lilies or water hyacinth covering a lake so thickly that boats cannot pass.
explanations.art: A lake with a thick green bloom on top, fertiliser sacks on the bank, and below the surface bare dying plants and a few fish at the bottom.

explanations.concept: Building up in bodies: from plankton to people
explanations.definition: Bioaccumulation is a pollutant building up inside a living body over time. When it passes up a food chain and grows stronger at each step, it is called biomagnification.
explanations.description: Some pollutants are not broken down or passed out of the body. Methylmercury is one. Tiny plankton take it in from the water. A small fish eats thousands of plankton and keeps all the mercury in them. A bigger fish eats many small fish and keeps theirs. A person or a heron at the end of the chain eats the biggest fish and gets the most. The water itself may have almost none. In the fish at the top there can be many thousands of times more. This is why pollution that looks tiny in a river can still harm the animals at the top of the food chain.
examples: Mercury in large fish such as swordfish and shark, which some countries warn pregnant women not to eat.
DDT, a pesticide, built up in birds at the top of food chains and thinned their eggshells. Rachel Carson warned about it in Silent Spring in 1962.
The Minamata story: cats, then people, fell ill from fish.
explanations.art: A food chain drawn left to right: plankton, a small fish, a big fish, a heron and a person, each with a bigger pile of dark dots drawn in the body.

explanations.concept: Why some pollution goes away and some does not
explanations.definition: Biodegradable waste is eaten by microbes and turned into simple things. An element, such as lead or mercury, cannot be broken down by anyone. It can only move, or be locked away.
explanations.description: Microbes are very good cooks. They can eat sewage, vegetable waste, cooking oil and even some oil spills. These are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen joined together in ways microbes have met for millions of years. But a mercury atom is an element. Nothing in a living body can turn it into something else. It can sit in mud, be washed to the sea or be swallowed by a fish, but the mercury stays mercury. Some plastics sit in between. Microbes have only just begun to meet them, and most have no way to eat them yet.
examples: A banana peel is food for microbes and rots away in weeks.
Lead from old petrol, once in the air, is still found in soil and in ice from long ago.
Most plastic bags last for many years, breaking into smaller pieces and not into soil.
explanations.art: Two paths from a cluster of atoms: on the left, microbes eating a peel and leaving soil and gas, on the right, a mercury atom going from mud to a fish and staying whole.

explanations.concept: Oil on water: contain it, soak it, skim it
explanations.definition: Oil is lighter than water and does not mix with it, so it spreads into a thin floating layer. Because it floats on top, it can be held in with a floating barrier, skimmed off, or soaked up.
explanations.description: A drop of oil on water spreads out wider and wider. The thinner it gets, the harder it is to collect. So the first job in a spill is to keep it from spreading. A boom is a long floating barrier, with a part above the water and a skirt below it. Then boats skim the oil from the top, or workers soak it up with materials that take in oil but not water. Detergent does not remove oil. It breaks the oil into tiny drops that mix through the water. Experts sometimes use special chemicals called dispersants to do this on purpose, and scientists argue about when that is wise.
examples: In January 2017, two ships collided off Ennore near Chennai and oil washed on to the beach. Many volunteers helped to scoop it up.
Floating booms around a ship that is being loaded with oil.
Mats of hair or sponge-like material used to soak up a spill.
explanations.art: A ship with a leaking hull, a floating orange boom curved around the black slick, and a small boat skimming oil from the surface.

explanations.concept: How a sewage treatment plant cleans water
explanations.definition: A sewage treatment plant cleans used water in stages. It takes out big bits, then lets solids settle, then lets microbes eat the waste, and last kills germs.
explanations.description: First, screens catch big things such as plastic and rags. Second, the water stands still in a tank and heavy bits settle as sludge. Third, air is bubbled through the water and microbes that breathe air eat the waste in the water. This is the stage that does most of the cleaning, and it is alive. Fourth, the cleaned water is disinfected with chlorine or ultraviolet light. The clean water can be used to flush toilets or water gardens, or it can be let into a river. The sludge is dried and used for compost. A plant cannot take out everything, and it cannot take out most dissolved chemicals from factories.
examples: Many large apartment blocks in Indian cities have a small treatment plant at the back, and use its water for gardens.
In the East Kolkata Wetlands, a Ramsar site, the city's sewage runs through shallow fish ponds, where algae and microbes clean it.
Reed beds, which are shallow ponds planted with reeds, clean small amounts of water in some villages and schools.
explanations.art: A row of four tanks: a screen catching rags, a settling tank with sludge at the bottom, a tank with air bubbles and microbes, and a tank with a chlorine pipe, water getting clearer.

explanations.concept: How we check water: tests and living signs
explanations.definition: No single test says whether water is clean. Each test checks one thing. Scientists use many tests, and also living beings that show the health of the water.
explanations.description: A turbidity test checks how cloudy the water is. A pH test checks how sour or soapy it is. A dissolved oxygen meter checks how much air the fish have. A coliform test checks for the bacteria found in human and animal waste, which means germs may be present. The Central Pollution Control Board gives rivers a best-use class, from A, which is drinking after disinfection, to E, which is only for irrigation and cooling. So 'clean' always means clean for a use. Streams also have living signs. Mayfly nymphs need clean, oxygen-rich water. Red sludge worms live in very dirty mud.
examples: A river stretch can pass the test for bathing and fail the test for drinking.
Finding mayfly nymphs under the stones of a hill stream means the water is rich in oxygen.
A coliform test on a village well after a flood.
explanations.art: A scientist with four test strips and a meter at a stream edge, and a small drawing of a mayfly nymph on a stone.

explanations.definition: Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres. Some are made that small, and most come from bigger plastic that has broken up.
explanations.description: A plastic bottle left in the sun and rain slowly cracks and breaks into smaller and smaller bits. Washing clothes made of polyester or nylon also sends tiny fibres into the drain. Scientists have found microplastics in the deepest ocean trench, in Himalayan snow, in tap water and in fish. In 2022 a team in the Netherlands reported plastic particles in the blood of most of the 22 people they tested. What this does to a body is still being studied. Nobody yet knows for sure. This is an idea we are still testing, and not a finished answer.
examples: Tiny fibres in the water from a washing machine.
Small bits of a bottle found in a river after a flood.
Microplastics have been found in sea salt, in some bottled water and in fish.
explanations.art: A plastic bottle on the left breaking into smaller and smaller pieces moving right across the page, ending as dots in a drop of water under a lens.

agreed.text: Thinning something out in water lowers how strong it is, but not how much of it there is.
agreed.evidence: Matter is not used up when it mixes. A chemist can still find the dye from one drop in a bathtub, using an instrument.

agreed.text: Untreated sewage is the biggest source of pollution in India's rivers.
agreed.evidence: The Central Pollution Control Board's river monitoring reports name sewage as the main source, and find that much of the sewage from towns and cities is not treated.

agreed.text: Waste that microbes can eat uses up the oxygen dissolved in water, and fish die when it runs low.
agreed.evidence: Dissolved oxygen meters show low readings in polluted water, and fish kills follow.

agreed.text: Some pollutants build up along a food chain, so animals at the top carry far more than the water does.
agreed.evidence: At Minamata in Japan, fish held far more mercury than the bay water. People and cats who ate the fish fell ill. Researchers at Kumamoto University traced the cause to mercury in 1959.

agreed.text: A sewage treatment plant takes out most solids, much of the microbe food and most germs. It takes out few of the dissolved chemicals from factories.
agreed.evidence: Plants measure the water before and after each stage, and report what is taken out.

agreed.text: Plastic breaks into smaller pieces, but does not rot away within a person's lifetime.
agreed.evidence: Plastic pieces have been found in the deepest ocean trenches, in mountain snow and in human blood.

challenging.claim: If water looks clear, it is clean.
challenging.who: Many people, and sometimes even people who run water supplies.
challenging.for: Muddy and green water are often dirty, and clear water is often fine to drink.
challenging.against: Salt, dye, petrol, many germs and chemicals such as arsenic and fluoride dissolve in water and leave it clear. Only a test can tell.

challenging.claim: A river or the sea is so big that it can take any amount of waste.
challenging.for: Rivers do clean themselves a little. Microbes eat natural waste, and the flowing water brings in fresh oxygen.
challenging.against: Some wastes do not break down, and they build up in mud and in animals. Too much waste even of the kind microbes can eat uses up all the oxygen.

challenging.claim: Boiling makes any water safe to drink.
challenging.who: Many families, and some health posters.
challenging.for: Boiling kills germs, such as the ones that cause cholera and typhoid.
challenging.against: Boiling does not remove dissolved chemicals such as pesticides, fluoride or arsenic. As the water boils away, the chemicals left behind get stronger.

challenging.claim: Dispersants, chemicals that break oil into droplets, are a good way to deal with a big oil spill at sea.
challenging.who: Some spill-response agencies, and some scientists.
challenging.for: The tiny droplets are eaten faster by microbes, and the oil stays off beaches and birds' feathers.
challenging.against: The oil is still in the water, and may harm fish and corals below. Scientists are still studying how much harm the dispersants add.

challenging.claim: A river can be a person in law, with rights of her own.
challenging.who: In 2017, the Whanganui River in New Zealand was given legal personhood. In the same year a High Court in Uttarakhand declared the Ganga and the Yamuna to be living entities.
challenging.for: A river cannot speak for herself, and today no one is made to answer for what is done to her. A guardian could speak for the river.
challenging.against: It is not clear who would be responsible, and who would pay if the river were harmed. The Supreme Court of India stopped the Uttarakhand order later in 2017.

big_questions.q: Your eyes say a glass of water is clean, and your nose says it is not. Which one is right, and who decides?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each check can find and what each check misses.

big_questions.q: A fish, a dog and a chemist's machine each check the same pond. Do they find the same water, or three different waters?
big_questions.hint: Think of a dog, who smells far more than you do, and a chemist's machine, which measures what no nose can. Are they seeing the same pond in different ways, or different ponds?

big_questions.q: Mercury is an element, and nothing alive can turn it into anything else. When we say we threw it 'away', where is away?
big_questions.hint: Follow the mercury from the factory pipe to the bay mud, to a fish, to a person.

big_questions.q: A factory's waste is too small to harm anyone in one day. Is it fair to let it go on for fifty years?
big_questions.hint: Think of a small amount of waste added every single day for fifty years, and where all of it goes.

big_questions.q: The cats of Minamata fell ill before the people did. Why was it so hard to listen to them?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets believed, who gets blamed and who has a company's name on their pay slip.

big_questions.q: In the East Kolkata Wetlands, the city's sewage feeds fish and vegetables. Is sewage waste, or is it food in the wrong place?
big_questions.hint: Think of what microbes, algae and fish do with it.

big_questions.q: Many people wash away their sins in a river and drink from it too. How can a river carry both a prayer and a pesticide?
big_questions.hint: Think about what 'carry away' means for the water and for the people downstream.

big_questions.q: If a river were allowed to take people to court, what would she ask for?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the river needs, and who would speak for her.

story.title: The Well You Could See Through
story.note: The story is made up, and so are the people and the village. The facts are true. Petrol floats on water, but a little of it dissolves, and a leaking underground tank at a petrol bunk can pollute a nearby well. People can smell petrol in water in tiny amounts, and a lab measures the exact amount.
text: Thamarai lived in a village between Madurai and Theni, in a house with a red-oxide floor and a well in the back yard. The well was older than her Paati. In all those years it had never run dry.

In the summer when Thamarai turned nine, the water began to smell. It was a faint smell, like a scooter that has just been switched off. She noticed it first when she filled the pot for rice. She sniffed the pot. She sniffed the tumbler. She even sniffed her own hands, in case the smell was theirs. It was in the water.
'Paati,' she said, 'the well water smells of petrol.'

Paati took the lamp and leaned over the wall of the well. The water below was green-black and still. She could see the old bricks going down, and the pale shape of a lost pot lid on the bottom. 'Kanna,' she said, 'I can see right to the bottom. Dirty water is brown. This water is clean. Your nose is confused by the heat.'

Thamarai did not argue. But she did not stop sniffing either. A year ago a petrol bunk had opened at the junction on the highway, with two bright pumps and a flag. The bunk stood uphill from their well. Thamarai remembered that, because her uncle had said the road was good for business.

The week before, in school, Gomathi Miss had made the class thin out coloured, scented water, one spoonful at a time. Thamarai remembered the third tumbler. It looked just like plain water, but it still smelled of vanilla. 'Your eyes give up first,' Gomathi Miss had said. 'Your nose keeps going a little longer. But only a measuring instrument keeps going all the way.'

That evening Thamarai tried something. She borrowed three steel tumblers that looked exactly alike. She filled two from the tap at the Panchayat tank, which came from a different source. She filled one from the well. Then she asked her little cousin Karthik to stand behind the door, shuffle the tumblers, and roll a die to decide where the well water would go.

'Paati,' she said, 'close your eyes. One of these is from the well. Sniff, and point.' Paati sighed and did it, to prove Thamarai wrong. She sniffed the first tumbler. She sniffed the second. She frowned at the third. Then she pointed straight at the right one.

'Again,' said Thamarai. Karthik shuffled. Paati pointed. Right. 'Again.' Right once more. Paati opened her eyes, and for a while she said nothing. 'Three out of three,' said Thamarai quietly. 'If you were only guessing, Paati, you would get all three right just one time in twenty-seven.'

The next morning they went to see Pushpam Akka, the Panchayat president. She did not laugh. She phoned the water-testing lab in the district town. Two days later a young scientist called Hameeda came in a white van, with a box of clean glass bottles and a pair of gloves. She filled one bottle from the well and one from the Panchayat tank, and sealed them both.

Ten days later the report came. Hameeda stood in the Panchayat office with the paper in her hand. 'There is petrol in your well,' she said. 'Not a lot. The water would look perfectly clear. But it is in there, and it is enough that nobody should drink it for years.' She looked at Thamarai. 'Your nose found it before my machine did. But a nose cannot tell how much, and some dangerous things have no smell at all. So we measure.'

The old underground tank at the petrol bunk had rusted through. It had been leaking slowly for months. Petrol floats on water, but a little of it dissolves, and a slow leak has all the time in the world. The owner, Mr Sivakumar, dug up the tank and paid for a tanker to bring water to the village until the well could be pumped clean. It took six months.
Thamarai still smells the well every morning. 'The eyes are good at finding what you can see,' she told Karthik. 'But clear only means the eyes found nothing. It does not mean there is nothing.'

And Paati, who had looked into that well for sixty years and trusted her eyes, now sniffs the water before she pours it for the rice. 'Not because my eyes are old,' she says. 'Because they are only one of the ways to look.'
story.epiphany: Clear only means the eyes found nothing. It does not mean there is nothing.
ask: How could you find out by testing, and not by arguing, whether a well has a smell?
A nose found the petrol and a machine measured it. What can each one do that the other cannot?
Who should check a village's water, and how often?
