games.title: Net, Cloth or Neither? Can you clean it out?
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card shows something in dirty water. You choose whether a net, a cloth, or neither can take it out.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, and a row of three verdict tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else puts a token face down.

setup.art: Three tokens turned over together, and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: something in dirty water on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A plastic bag floating on a pond.
items.b: Net or skimmer. It floats and it is big, so a net lifts it out.

items.f: Mud washed into a stream by monsoon rain.
items.b: Settle, then cloth. Mud grains sink if the water stands still, and a cloth catches the grains that are left.

items.f: Salt dissolved in a tumbler of water.
items.b: Neither works. Dissolved salt is split into single tiny pieces. No net or cloth can hold them. Evaporation or special filters are needed.

items.f: Coconut shells and flower garlands left floating on a lake after a festival.
items.b: Net or skimmer. They float and they are big, so a net or a boat with a skimmer can lift them out.

items.f: The brown colour that has dissolved in a cup of tea.
items.b: Neither works. The tea leaves can be strained out, but the colour is dissolved and passes through any strainer.

items.f: Tea leaves floating in a cup of tea.
items.b: Net or skimmer. A tea strainer is a tiny net. It catches the big bits.

items.f: Fine silt from a building site that makes rainwater cloudy.
items.b: Settle, then cloth. Silt sinks slowly when the water is still. A cloth then catches what is left.

items.f: Cooking oil in a thin layer on a bowl of water.
items.b: Net or skimmer. Oil floats. A spoon, a skimmer or a pad that soaks up oil can lift it, though a thin film is hard to get.

items.f: Fertiliser dissolved in the water of a farm pond.
items.b: Neither works. Dissolved plant food is too small for any cloth. It has to be kept out of the water in the first place.

items.f: Detergent dissolved in the water from a washing machine.
items.b: Neither works. The foam can be skimmed off, but the detergent stays dissolved in the water.

items.f: Dead leaves floating on a stream.
items.b: Net or skimmer. They float and they are big, so a net lifts them out.

items.f: Turmeric powder stirred into a glass of water so that it turns yellow and cloudy.
items.b: Settle, then cloth. The grains are tiny and sink slowly. Left alone they settle, and a cloth or paper filter catches the rest.

items.f: A pesticide dissolved in runoff from a field.
items.b: Neither works. A dissolved chemical goes through a net and a cloth. Charcoal or special treatment is needed.

items.f: Dye dissolved in the waste water from a cloth-dyeing factory.
items.b: Neither works. Dissolved dye is too small to catch. The factory has to treat the water before it goes out.

items.f: Pieces of thermocol floating on a lake.
items.b: Net or skimmer. They float and are big, so a net lifts them out.

items.f: Germs from sewage swimming in a pond.
items.b: Neither works. The gaps in a cloth are far wider than a germ. Chlorine, ultraviolet light or boiling kills germs.

items.f: Sand stirred up by a flood in a river.
items.b: Settle, then cloth. Sand sinks within a minute when the water is still, and a cloth catches any that is left.

items.f: Hot water from a factory, warm enough to harm fish.
items.b: Neither works. Heat is not a bit that can be caught. The water has to cool down before it goes out.

items.f: Used engine oil from a garage, floating as a rainbow shine on a puddle.
items.b: Net or skimmer. Oil floats, so it can be skimmed or soaked up from the top.

items.f: Rice husk and straw floating on a canal.
items.b: Net or skimmer. They float and they are big, so a net lifts them out.

items.f: Arsenic dissolved in well water in parts of the Ganga plains.
items.b: Neither works. It is dissolved, and the water looks clear and has no smell. Special filters, or another water source, are needed.

items.f: Chalk dust shaken into a bucket of water.
items.b: Settle, then cloth. The dust sinks slowly. A cloth or filter paper catches what is left once it settles.

items.f: Plastic bottles and rubbish stuck at a drain grill.
items.b: Net or skimmer. They are big and they float or stick, so a net or a rake lifts them out.

items.f: Sugar dissolved in sweet water from a sweet-making shop.
items.b: Neither works. Dissolved sugar goes straight through any cloth. It is also food for microbes, which can use up the oxygen in the water.

printables.title: 12 verdict tokens: four sets of three

rules: Net or skimmer means a net, a strainer or a skimmer can lift it out. Settle, then cloth means it sinks when the water is still, and a cloth catches what is left. Neither works means it is dissolved, too small, or not a thing at all, so a net or a cloth cannot take it out.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Each player whose token matches the first words of the back scores one point.
The reader's role passes round after each card. The winner is the player with the most points when the cards run out.
Playing alone: draw a card, put down a token, then turn the card over and read the back. Try to score 18 out of 24.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show things in dirty water. Each player gets three tokens. We guess whether a net, a cloth, or neither can take it out.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Net, Cloth or Neither. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: Cutting 36 pieces takes a while, and young children need care with scissors, so a parent can cut the cards while the child cuts the tokens. With 2 to 4 players, one child reads at a time. Alone, play both parts.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after the third card.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else picks a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: Why do you think a net or a cloth could not catch that one?
good: It is dissolved.
It is too small.
It is a germ, which is alive.
It floats, so a cloth is not needed.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to guess.

flow.do: Play the next twelve cards. Keep score. After the sixth card of this round, ask the question below.
flow.say: Keep going. Keep your own score. Is there a pattern in what a net can catch, and what it cannot?
flow.kid: Keep playing. Keep your score. Is there a pattern?

ask.q: What do the Neither works cards have in common?
good: They are dissolved.
They are too small to see.
Most of them are clear.

flow.parent: Most Neither works cards are dissolved things, germs, or heat. The cards that a net can catch float, and the cards that need a cloth sink. The clear point is that dissolved pollution cannot be seen and cannot be caught.
flow.context: In this step, you play more cards and look for the pattern.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. Add up the scores. Ask your child which kinds of pollution are the hardest to clean, and which kinds are the easiest.
flow.say: Play the last six cards and count up your points. Which kind of dirt is the hardest to clean up? Which is the easiest? Why?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points. Which dirt is hardest to clean?
flow.parent: Cleaning is hardest for the things that cannot be seen. That is why the best answer is not to put them in the water at all.
flow.think: Why is it better to keep dissolved things out of the water than to clean them out afterwards?
flow.context: This is the last step of Net, Cloth or Neither. You count the points and think about which dirt is hardest to clean.

experiments.title: Gone from Sight: where do the colour and the smell stop?
experiments.question: If we thin coloured, scented water again and again, in which tumbler does the colour stop showing to the eye, and in which does the smell stop showing to the nose? Is the colour gone when we can no longer see it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which tumbler will the colour vanish? In which will the smell vanish? Which goes first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every tumbler holds the same 200 millilitres of clean water, and every step uses one level teaspoon. Tumbler 0 is the control: no colour and no essence. Each tumbler is looked at in the same light, on the same white paper. In the sniff test, a die picks where the odd cup goes, the child's eyes are shut, and tumblers 2, 3 and 4 are each tried three times, because one try can be a fluke. Rest your nose for a minute between rounds.
results_table: Can you see colour? (yes or no)

materials.item: 5 clear tumblers or glasses of the same size
about 1.2 litres of clean drinking water, and a jug
5 drops of food colour (red, blue or green)
1 teaspoon of food essence such as vanilla, rose or kewra
a teaspoon, and a small bowl of water for rinsing it
3 identical small cups, such as paper cups or steel katoris
a die, a sheet of white paper, a marker pen and sticky labels
a book or a cloth to hide the cups, and the results table

experiments.safety: Do not drink or taste anything in the tumblers. Food essence is strong, so keep it away from eyes and from small children. Wash hands afterwards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the five tumblers in a row and colour each one as you saw it. Mark the tumbler where the colour stopped and the tumbler where the smell stopped.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you thin coloured, scented water again and again. You find out where your eyes stop noticing the colour, and where your nose stops noticing the smell.

setup.art: Five clear tumblers in a row, numbered 0 to 4, each holding 200 millilitres of clean water, with a jug beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Number five tumblers 0 to 4. Pour 200 millilitres of clean water into each.

setup.art: Five drops of red food colour and a teaspoon of essence going into tumbler 1, with tumbler 0 left plain.
setup.caption: 2. Add 5 drops of colour and 1 teaspoon of essence to tumbler 1 only. Stir.

setup.art: A level teaspoon carrying water from tumbler 1 to tumbler 2, with curved arrows then going from 2 to 3 and from 3 to 4.
setup.caption: 3. Move one level spoonful from tumbler 1 to 2, then from 2 to 3, then from 3 to 4. Rinse the spoon each time.

setup.art: The five tumblers in a row on white paper, from bright red to plain-looking water.
setup.caption: 4. Look at each tumbler beside tumbler 0. Is there any colour?

setup.art: A child with closed eyes sniffing one of three identical cups, while a parent behind a book shuffles them and holds a die.
setup.caption: 5. Eyes shut, sniff three cups. Two are plain and one is from tumbler 2, then 3, then 4. Point to the one that smells.

flow.do: Show the five numbered tumblers, the colour and the essence. Explain the plan. Write down your child's guess and the reason for it.
flow.say: We will make coloured, scented water, and then thin it out again and again. In which tumbler will the colour vanish? In which will the smell vanish? Which goes first, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will thin out coloured, scented water again and again. Where will the colour vanish? Where will the smell vanish? Which goes first, and why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one goes first?
good: Eyes need a strong colour to see it.
Smells travel in the air, so the nose finds them easily.
I do not know, so let us test it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Wait for a place and a reason. Write both at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gone from Sight. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Label five tumblers 0 to 4 with a marker or a sticker. Pour 200 millilitres of clean water into each. Leave tumbler 0 plain. Add 5 drops of food colour and 1 teaspoon of essence to tumbler 1. Stir well.
flow.say: Pour clean water into all five tumblers, 200 millilitres each. Tumbler 0 stays plain. It is our control, the water we compare with. Into tumbler 1 go five drops of colour and one teaspoon of essence. Stir it well.
flow.kid: Pour 200 millilitres of water into each tumbler. Leave tumbler 0 plain. Put the colour and essence into tumbler 1. Stir.
flow.parent: Any food essence works, for example vanilla, rose or kewra. A fresh bottle is stronger than an old one. Level the teaspoon with a knife. If you have no food colour, use two tablespoons of strong tea that has cooled. With 2 to 4 children: one pours and labels, one stirs and measures with the spoon, and everyone swaps for the next tumbler. A level spoon is 5 millilitres. If you have no measuring spoon, a clean medicine cap or a steel teaspoon levelled with a knife is close enough. The sniff cups need no extra kit; steel katoris are fine if they are washed with no soap smell.

check.q: Why does tumbler 0 get no colour and no essence?
options: So we have plain water to compare with
To save colour
Because it is the last tumbler
check.why: A control is the same as the others in everything except the thing you test. Tumbler 0 shows what plain water looks and smells like. So any difference in the other tumblers comes from the colour and the essence.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the five tumblers and make the strong mix in tumbler 1.

flow.do: Take one level teaspoon from tumbler 1 and stir it into tumbler 2. Rinse the spoon. Take one teaspoon from tumbler 2 into tumbler 3. Stir and rinse. Take one teaspoon from tumbler 3 into tumbler 4. Stir and rinse.
flow.say: Now we thin it out. One spoonful from tumbler 1 goes into tumbler 2. Stir. Rinse the spoon. Then one spoonful from 2 goes into 3, and one from 3 goes into 4.
flow.kid: Take one spoon from tumbler 1. Stir it into tumbler 2. Rinse the spoon. Do the same from 2 to 3, then 3 to 4.
flow.parent: Rinse the spoon in the bowl, never in the tumblers. A level spoon holds 5 millilitres. It lands in 200 millilitres, so the tumbler then holds 205 millilitres. That makes each tumbler 41 times weaker than the one before.

check.q: One spoonful of tumbler 1 goes into 200 millilitres of clean water. How much weaker is tumbler 2 than tumbler 1?
options: 41 times weaker
2 times weaker
The same strength
check.why: The spoonful holds 5 millilitres and ends up in 205 millilitres. 205 divided by 5 is 41. So the colour and the scent in tumbler 2 are spread 41 times thinner.

flow.context: In this step, you thin the mix out four times. Each tumbler gets weaker.

flow.do: Stand the tumblers in a row on white paper, in daylight. Look at each from the side and from above. Compare each with tumbler 0. Write yes or no for colour in the table.
flow.say: Look at each tumbler next to tumbler 0. Is there any colour at all? Say yes or no, and I will write it down. Which is the first tumbler with no colour?
flow.kid: Line the tumblers up on white paper. Compare each with tumbler 0. Is there colour? Write yes or no.

ask.q: Look at the first tumbler with no colour. Is the colour really gone?
good: It looks gone, but I am not sure.
It is just too thin for me to see.
I think it is still in there.

flow.parent: Do not hurry. Hold tumbler 0 right beside each tumbler. Some children say 'no colour' as soon as the colour is very pale. Write what they see, even if it is not what they guessed.
flow.context: In this step, you use your eyes to find where the colour stops.

flow.do: Set out three identical small cups. Pour 2 tablespoons from tumbler 0 into two of them. Pour 2 tablespoons from tumbler 2 into the third. Roll a die to pick the place of the odd cup. A 1 or 2 means left, 3 or 4 means middle, and 5 or 6 means right. Your child shuts their eyes, sniffs all three and points to the one that smells. Write right or wrong. Do three trials with tumbler 2, then three with tumbler 3, then three with tumbler 4.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will put three cups in front of you. Two are plain water and one is from tumbler 2. Sniff each one. Point to the one that smells. Do not tell me why until the end. Then we try tumbler 3, and then tumbler 4.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Sniff the three cups. Point to the one that smells. Then we do it again.

ask.q: How sure are you? Did you smell it, or guess?
good: I smelled something faint.
I guessed.
One cup was different, but I cannot say how.

flow.parent: Do not look at the child, and give no hints with your face. Roll the die again for each trial, so the odd cup moves around. Rinse and dry the cups between trials. Tumbler 2 is the easy warm-up and most noses find it. Tumbler 3 is near the edge: some noses find it and some do not, and tumbler 4 is usually too weak for anyone. Rose and kewra essence are stronger than vanilla, and a fresh bottle is stronger than an old one. If even tumbler 2 has no smell, your essence is weak, so write that down and compare tumbler 1 with tumbler 0 instead. With several children, each takes a turn as the sniffer while another rolls the die and arranges the cups, and the others stay out of sight. Where your child's nose stops is the result, whichever tumbler it is.

check.q: Three cups, and only one has the scent. If a child just guesses, how often will they point to the right cup?
options: 1 time in 3
1 time in 2
Every time
check.why: With three cups and one odd cup, a pure guess is right one time in three. Three right guesses in a row by luck would be rare: 1 time in 27. So getting all three right means the nose really found it.

flow.context: In this step, you use your nose to find where the smell stops. A die makes the test fair.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I thought. What I saw and smelled. Why I think it happened. Then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see and smell? Why do you think the colour and the smell stopped where they did?
flow.kid: Say three things. What did you think? What did you see and smell? Why did it happen?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the colour was too thin for the eyes by tumbler 3 (often by tumbler 2 on a white background), while the nose could still find the scent in tumbler 2 and sometimes in tumbler 3. So the eyes gave up before the nose did, and tumbler 3 was not plain water even though it looks like it. If your child's nose gave up at tumbler 2, say that it just means the scent was thinner for that nose. Each tumbler is far more than 41 times thinner than the first, so the stuff is certainly still there. After the child has said this, add that a chemist's instrument can go on finding things long after the nose gives up. Neither eyes nor nose are measuring tools.
flow.think: Tumbler 3 looks like plain water. Is it plain water?

check.q: Suppose a tumbler of thinned scented water looks like plain water, but a nose picks it out three times out of three. What does this show?
options: The scent is still there. The eyes stopped finding it before the nose did.
The colour made the scent stronger.
Tumbler 3 is the same as plain water.
check.why: Eyes found nothing, but the nose did, so something was still in the water. Looking is only one way of checking. If you picked the second option, remember that the colour and the scent are two separate things in the same water.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you thought, what you found, and why.

flow.do: Ask where the five drops of colour are now. Then tip the tumblers into the sink and wash up.
flow.say: We began with five drops of colour. Where are they now?
flow.kid: Where are the five drops of colour now?

ask.q: Where are the five drops of colour now?
good: Spread out through all the tumblers.
Most of them are still in tumbler 1.
They are still somewhere, just too thin to see.

flow.parent: Most of the colour is still in tumbler 1, because each spoonful took only one forty-first of it. The rest is spread out, thinner at each step. Nothing was destroyed. It was only spread out. You can say this after your child has answered.
flow.context: This is the last step of Gone from Sight. You think about where the colour went.

experiments.title: The Overnight Collector: can a paper strip find what your eyes cannot?
experiments.question: A tumbler of water looks almost clear. If a paper strip hangs in it overnight, does the strip collect the hidden colour near its top? What about a tumbler where you saw no colour at all?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which tumbler will the strip show colour in the morning? In which will it show none? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The three tumblers each hold 200 millilitres. The strips are the same paper, the same size, and dip the same 2 centimetres. One tumbler holds plain water, as the control. The tumbler marked 'tint' is the last one in which you could see a faint colour. The tumbler marked 'none' is the first one in which you saw no colour. All three stand in the same place overnight.
results_table: Colour on the strip? (none, faint or clear)
Height of the colour from the water (cm)

materials.item: 3 clear tumblers from the Gone from Sight test: plain water, the last tumbler with a tint, and the first tumbler with no colour
3 strips of thick white kitchen tissue or coffee filter paper (a plain paper napkin also works), 2 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres long
3 pencils or ice-cream sticks, and sticky tape (a fourth strip and pencil are useful, see the notes)
a ruler, a marker pen, and the results table

experiments.safety: Do not drink the water. Wash hands after handling the coloured strips. Make the tumblers again if you did the first test more than a day ago.
experiments.record: Write what each strip looks like in the morning, and measure how high any colour has climbed. Draw the three strips side by side.
experiments.context: In this experiment, a paper strip hangs in nearly clear water overnight. You find out whether the strip can collect colour that the eyes cannot see in the tumbler.

setup.art: Three tumblers labelled plain, tint and none, each with a long white paper strip taped to a pencil that lies across the rim, and the bottom 2 centimetres of the strip dipping into the water.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a strip to a pencil. Rest the pencil on the rim so that the strip dips 2 centimetres in the water.

setup.art: A close-up of one strip with water climbing up it, a ruler beside it, and the wet part darker than the dry part.
setup.caption: 2. Water climbs the paper by itself. Put the tumblers in a breezy spot, and leave them overnight.

setup.art: The same strips taken out in the morning and laid side by side on a plate, one with a coloured band near its top.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, lay the strips side by side. Look for colour near the top of each.

schedule.what: Guess. Make the three tumblers if needed. Hang the strips and leave them overnight in a breezy spot.
Take out the strips. Compare them. Measure where any colour has climbed. Say what you found and why.

flow.do: Show the three tumblers and the paper strips. Explain that the strips will hang in the water overnight. Write down your child's guess and the reason.
flow.say: Here are three tumblers, and each gets a paper strip. One tumbler has plain water, one has a very faint tint, and one looks like plain water. In which will the strip show colour tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three tumblers get a paper strip each. In which will the strip show colour tomorrow? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that strip will show colour?
good: Water climbs up the paper and leaves the colour behind.
The paper drinks the colour.
I am not sure, so let us test it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. Use the tumblers from the Gone from Sight test, or make a new row of five and use tumbler 0, the last tint and the first one with no colour.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Overnight Collector. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut three strips, 2 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres long. Tape the top of each strip to a pencil. Rest each pencil across a tumbler so that the strip dips 2 centimetres in the water. Mark the water level with the marker. Write the labels plain, tint and none on the tumblers.
flow.say: Tape each strip to a pencil. Lay the pencil across the tumbler. The strip should just dip into the water, about two centimetres. Label the tumblers plain, tint and none.
flow.kid: Tape a strip to a pencil. Lay the pencil across a tumbler. Dip the strip 2 centimetres. Label the tumblers.
flow.parent: The strip must hang free and not touch the glass. If it touches, the water can creep down the glass instead. Make sure all three strips are cut from the same sheet of paper. With 2 to 4 children, each child can cut, tape and hang one strip, and the fourth child can read out the labels. If you have a spare strip, hang it in the strong tumbler 1 as a sure-to-work comparison.

check.q: Why do all three strips dip the same 2 centimetres?
options: So the only difference is the water in the tumbler
To make the strips wet quickly
Because paper is easier to cut that way
check.why: If one strip dipped deeper, any difference we saw might come from that. A fair test changes one thing only, and here that one thing is the water in the tumbler.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the strips in the three tumblers.

flow.do: Put the three tumblers on a plate in a breezy place, such as by a window or in a gentle fan's breeze. Leave them overnight. Do not move them.
flow.say: Put the tumblers somewhere with moving air, by a window or in the breeze of a slow fan. Leave them overnight. We will look in the morning.
flow.kid: Put the tumblers in a breezy spot. Leave them overnight. Do not touch them.
flow.parent: Moving air makes the water dry off the strip faster. As water dries off the top of the strip, more climbs up to replace it and brings its colour along. The colour stays when the water leaves. In damp or rainy weather the strip dries off slowly, so put the tumblers right in front of a fan and give them 24 hours instead of overnight. If the strip has dried out completely and never climbed, check that it dips into the water.
flow.wait: Leave it overnight, for at least 8 hours.
flow.context: In this step, you leave the strips alone, so the water can climb the paper and dry off the top.

flow.do: Take out the strips and lay them side by side on a white plate. Look for colour near the top of each one. Write none, faint or clear. Measure the height of any colour from the water line. Look at each tumbler again beside the plain one.
flow.say: Lay the three strips side by side. Is there colour on any of them? Where is it? Write none, faint or clear for each one.
flow.kid: Lay the strips side by side. Is there colour? Where? Write none, faint or clear.

ask.q: Which strip has the most colour? Why do you think that is?
good: The one from the tint tumbler.
The paper collected it as the water dried.
The strip from the plain water has none.

flow.parent: Food colour often climbs as a band, and some colours split into two bands. Expect the strip from the 'tint' tumbler to show a pale but clear band near the top, even though the water in the tumbler looks almost clear. The strip from the 'none' tumbler is much harder: it may show a very faint tinge or nothing at all. Both are honest results, and nothing at all means the colour there was too thin even for a strip in one night. If even the 'tint' strip stays white, your colour was weak, so leave the strips for another night or make the tint with more drops.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the strips in the morning and write what you see.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they found and why. Then read the note together.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you find on the strips? Why do you think the colour ended up there?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you found and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that water climbed the strip and dried off near the top, and that the colour stayed behind and piled up there. The colour in the tumbler was too thin to see, but the strip collected it from a lot of water. After they say this, add that scientists often use mussels as living collectors for the same reason.
flow.think: Mussels filter a lot of water and keep what they cannot break down. How is a mussel like your strip?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Overnight Collector. You say what you thought and what the strips showed.

experiments.title: Oil Spill Race: which tool clears the most oil?
experiments.question: Which of five tools clears the most oil from a bowl of water in two minutes: a spoon, a paper towel, cotton wool, a tuft of hair or a drop of dishwash liquid? Does any of them leave the water truly oil-free?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which tool will clear the oil best, and which will do worst? Will any tool leave the water oil-free? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Six bowls each hold 300 millilitres of water and 1 tablespoon of the same oil. One bowl is left alone, as the control. Each tool works for exactly two minutes by the timer, and the same person works every tool. Afterwards a sample of water from just below the surface of each bowl is dropped on brown paper and left to dry. Oil leaves a see-through spot on paper, and plain water does not.
results_table: Shine left after 2 minutes (0 none, 5 as much as the control)
Oil spot on the paper from the water below the surface? (none, faint or clear)

materials.item: 6 shallow bowls or plates with a rim, all the same size, about 18 centimetres across
about 2 litres of water
6 tablespoons of cooking oil, any kind
a teaspoon, a sheet of paper towel, a handful of cotton wool, and a small tuft of clean hair from a comb
dishwash liquid, a few drops
a sheet of brown paper (a paper bag or envelope cut open) or plain white paper, and 6 drinking straws
a timer (a phone clock), a tray, old newspaper, an old container with a lid for the oily water, a marker pen and the results table

experiments.safety: Oil on the floor is slippery, so work on a tray over newspaper. Never pour oily water down the sink, because oil blocks pipes and is hard to clean. Pour it into an old container. Wipe the bowls with paper and put the paper in the dustbin. Keep dishwash liquid away from eyes, and wash hands after. If anyone is allergic to groundnut, use sunflower or mustard oil and keep the hair and cotton away from faces. Do not suck on the straws.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Score the shine by looking at each bowl from a low angle, with light behind it. Compare it with the control bowl, which scores 5.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you spill oil on water and race five different tools to clear it. You find out whether anything can get all the oil out.

setup.art: Six same-sized bowls in two rows on a tray, each with water and a golden patch of oil floating on top, one labelled control.
setup.caption: 1. Put 300 millilitres of water and 1 tablespoon of oil in each of six bowls.

setup.art: A child skimming oil with a spoon, a paper towel resting on another bowl, cotton wool on a third, a tuft of hair on a fourth, and a drop of dishwash liquid going into a fifth.
setup.caption: 2. Use a different tool on each of five bowls for exactly two minutes. Leave the sixth alone.

setup.art: A child looking across a bowl at a low angle towards a window to see the shine on the water.
setup.caption: 3. Look across each bowl from a low angle. Score how much shine is left, from 0 to 5.

setup.art: A drinking straw held shut with a thumb dipping below the oil in a bowl, and then six drops on brown paper drying in a row with a see-through spot on one of them.
setup.caption: 4. With a straw closed by your thumb, take a sample from below the surface of each bowl. Drop it on paper and let it dry. Look for a see-through spot.

flow.do: Show the six bowls and the five tools. Explain that each tool gets two minutes. Write down your child's guess and the reason for it.
flow.say: We will spill oil on six bowls of water, and then clear it with five different tools. One bowl is left alone. Which tool will clear the oil best? Which will do worst? Will any tool leave the water oil-free? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will clear oil from water with five tools. Which works best? Which works worst? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that tool will work best?
good: It soaks up the oil.
It lifts the oil off the top.
Soap washes oil away.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect dishwash liquid to win, since it cleans greasy plates. Write the guess and the reason down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Oil Spill Race. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Number the bowls 1 to 6. Pour 300 millilitres of water into each. Add 1 tablespoon of oil to each. Label bowl 6 control. Match the tools to the bowls: 1 spoon, 2 paper towel, 3 cotton wool, 4 hair, 5 dishwash liquid.
flow.say: Pour water into all six bowls. Add a tablespoon of oil to each. Watch how the oil spreads. Bowl 6 is the control, so we will not touch it.
flow.kid: Pour water into six bowls. Add a spoon of oil to each. Watch how it spreads. Bowl 6 is the control.

ask.q: What does the oil do when it hits the water?
good: It floats.
It spreads out into a round patch.
It does not mix.

flow.parent: Pour the oil slowly onto the middle of the water. Oil floats because it is lighter than water, and it does not mix with water. Over a minute it spreads into a thin round patch.
flow.context: In this step, you make six small oil spills.

flow.do: Start the timer for bowl 1. Skim with the spoon for exactly two minutes. Stop. Then do bowl 2 with the paper towel, dabbing and replacing the squares. Do bowl 3 with cotton wool and bowl 4 with the tuft of hair. For bowl 5, add 3 drops of dishwash liquid and stir with the spoon for 10 seconds. Leave bowl 6 alone.
flow.say: Time two minutes for each bowl. Bowl 1, the spoon. Bowl 2, paper towel. Bowl 3, cotton wool. Bowl 4, hair. Bowl 5, three drops of dishwash liquid and a ten-second stir. Do not touch bowl 6.
flow.kid: Two minutes per bowl. Use the tool on its bowl. Do not touch bowl 6.

ask.q: What do you notice about the oil in bowl 5 after the dishwash liquid?
good: It breaks into lots of little drops.
It moved to the sides.
The water looks cloudy.

flow.parent: Use the same effort for each tool. Dishwash liquid usually pushes the oil to the edges first, and the stirring then breaks it into small drops that spread through the water. Squeeze the paper towel and cotton wool over the spare container, not over the bowls. With 2 to 4 children: one child works the tools one after another, one keeps the timer, one scores and writes. If you want every child to try, repeat with fresh bowls and swap jobs; the scores will differ a little, and that is worth talking about.
flow.context: In this step, you race the five tools, two minutes each.

flow.do: Look across each bowl from a low angle, with a window behind it. Score the shine from 0 to 5. The control bowl scores 5. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Look across each bowl from a low angle. How much shine is left on the water? Give it a score from 0 to 5. The control bowl is 5.
flow.kid: Look across each bowl. How much shine is left? Score 0 to 5.
flow.parent: Scores are a judgement, so ask the same person to score every bowl. A thin rainbow film still counts as shine. A bowl with tiny drops all over scores more than a bowl with a clean surface.

check.q: Why do we leave bowl 6 untouched?
options: It shows how much shine there is with no tool at all
To save oil
To have an extra bowl
check.why: The control shows what the spill looks like with no clean-up. Without it we could not say how much any tool took away.

flow.context: In this step, you score how much oil each tool left behind.

flow.do: Hold a clean straw shut with your thumb. Push it 3 centimetres under the surface in the middle of a bowl. Lift your thumb for a second, then close it. Lift the straw out and wipe the outside with a tissue. Let the water fall on one spot of the paper, twice. Label the spot with the bowl number. Use a new straw for every bowl. Let the paper dry for 15 to 20 minutes, near a fan if the air is damp. Then hold it up to the light and look for a see-through spot.
flow.say: Take a little water from just under the surface of each bowl with a straw, and drop it on the paper. Oil makes paper see-through when it dries. Water does not. Let us see which bowls have oil down in the water, below the shine.
flow.kid: Dip a paper strip in each bowl. Let it dry. Look for see-through spots.

ask.q: A bowl looks clear, but its strip has a see-through spot. What does that tell us?
good: There is still oil in the water.
Our eyes cannot find it all.
The tool did not get all the oil.

flow.parent: Bowls 1 to 4 have oil only on top, so their paper usually stays plain, or shows only a faint spot. Bowl 5 is the surprise. The surface looks cleaner, but the stirred-in oil has been broken into tiny drops that sit in the water, so its paper usually shows a see-through spot. If bowl 5 shows no spot, stir longer and sample again. Do not skip the control: bowl 6 should show no spot, because its oil is all on top. Write what you really see.
flow.context: In this step, you test each bowl for hidden oil with a paper strip.
flow.wait: Leave the paper to dry for 15 to 20 minutes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then read the note together.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think the tools worked the way they did?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says which tool left the least shine, and that the straw samples showed the oil in bowl 5 had not gone anywhere. After the child has said this, explain that skimming and soaking take oil out. Dishwash liquid does not. It splits oil into tiny drops that spread through the water, so the top looks clean while the water is not.
flow.think: Dishwash liquid made the surface look cleaner. Did it take the oil out of the water?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you thought, what you found, and why.

flow.do: Pour the oily water into the old container. Wipe the bowls with paper. Put the paper in the dustbin. Wash hands.
flow.say: Pour the oily water into the container, not down the sink. Wipe the bowls with paper. Put the paper in the dustbin.
flow.kid: Pour the oily water into the container. Wipe the bowls with paper. Wash your hands.
flow.parent: Close the container and put it out with the dry waste, or give it to a collector of used cooking oil if one comes to your area.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Oil Spill Race. You clean up, and do not send the oil down the drain.

activities.title: The Torch Beam Test: can a light show what clear water hides?

materials.item: 3 clear tumblers of the same size
600 millilitres of clean water
1 teaspoon of salt
a little milk, and a toothpick
a phone torch or a small torch (a bright, narrow beam works best; hold a card with a small hole over the front if the beam is wide)
a room that can be made dark, such as a bedroom in the evening with curtains drawn

activities.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Do not drink the water.
activities.record: Write beam, faint beam or no beam for each tumbler. Draw the three tumblers with the light going through them.
activities.context: In this activity, you shine a torch through three tumblers of clear-looking water. You find out which kinds of hidden dirt a beam of light can show up.

setup.art: Three clear tumblers in a row labelled A, B and C, each with 200 millilitres of water, with salt being stirred into B and a toothpick tip of milk being swirled into C.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three tumblers. Stir a teaspoon of salt into B. Swirl a toothpick tip of milk into C.

setup.art: A dark room with a torch beam shining sideways through a tumbler of water, and a bright streak glowing in the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. In a dark room, shine the torch through the side of each tumbler.

setup.art: A child's view of the three tumblers from the side, with a bright beam in C and almost no beam in A and B.
setup.caption: 3. Look from the side. Is the beam visible in the water?

flow.do: Show the three tumblers. Tell your child what goes in each. Ask in which tumbler a torch beam will show up. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Tumbler A is plain tap water. Tumbler B has salt dissolved in it. Tumbler C has a tiny drop of milk. In which will you see a beam of light? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A is plain water. B has salt. C has a drop of milk. Where will you see the beam? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that tumbler will show the beam?
good: Milk is white and cloudy.
Salt makes the water thick.
Clear water lets light through without showing it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Torch Beam Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 200 millilitres of water into each tumbler. Stir a level teaspoon of salt into B until you cannot see it. Dip the end of a toothpick in milk and swirl it in C. Stir C gently.
flow.say: Pour water into three tumblers. Stir a teaspoon of salt into B until it disappears. Dip a toothpick in milk and swirl it in C.
flow.kid: Fill three tumblers. Stir salt into B. Swirl a drop of milk into C.
flow.parent: One toothpick tip of milk is enough. Too much milk makes the water white and the beam cannot go through. If C looks white, pour half out and add water.
flow.context: In this step, you make the three tumblers.

flow.do: Make the room dark. Hold the torch against the side of tumbler A. Look from the side, not into the light. Write what you see. Do the same for B and C.
flow.say: Make the room dark. Shine the torch through the side of each tumbler, and look at it from the side. Is there a glowing beam inside the water? Write beam, faint beam or no beam.
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Shine the torch through each tumbler. Look from the side. Is there a beam?
flow.parent: Tumbler C should glow with a clear bluish streak. Tumbler B should look like tumbler A. Tap water may show a faint streak if it carries fine specks. That is a result too. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the torch, one holds the tumbler still, and the others look from the side. Swap for each tumbler. If the room is not dark, a cupboard or the space under a blanket works too.

check.q: In tumbler B the beam did not show, though there is salt in the water. What does this tell us?
options: Dissolved salt is too small to scatter the light
Salt water is the same as milk water
The torch was too weak
check.why: A beam shows up when tiny bits of milk or dust scatter the light towards your eyes. Dissolved salt is split into single tiny pieces that scatter almost no light. So a beam can show floating bits, but it cannot show dissolved things.

flow.context: In this step, you shine the torch through each tumbler and look for a beam.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found and why. Ask what the torch can find and what it cannot.
flow.say: Which tumbler showed the beam? Why? What kind of hidden dirt can a torch find, and what kind can it not find?
flow.kid: Which tumbler showed the beam? Why? What can a torch not find?
flow.parent: A strong answer says the beam showed up in the milk because milk is made of tiny bits floating in the water, and that it did not show up in the salt water because salt is dissolved. So the torch finds floating bits, but not dissolved things. After they say this, add that a torch beam is one more check, and like the eyes it misses some things.
flow.think: Water from a pond looks clear, and the beam shows nothing. Is the water clean?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Torch Beam Test. You say what a torch beam can and cannot find.

activities.title: Pass-It-On Seeds: how a little becomes a lot up a food chain

materials.item: 30 black seeds, such as whole black urad dal or black peppercorns
a sheet of paper with 30 squares drawn on it, 6 across and 5 down
6 small bowls or katoris
2 larger bowls
1 plate
a pencil

activities.safety: Keep the seeds away from small children and from mouths and noses. Do not eat the seeds after the game.
activities.record: Write how many seeds were in one plankton square, in one small fish bowl, in one big fish bowl and on the person's plate. Then write how many times more the person's plate holds than one plankton.
activities.context: In this activity, you act out how a small amount of a pollutant that the body cannot get rid of builds up along a food chain. Each black seed stands for a tiny bit of pollution.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with 30 squares, each with one black seed in it, labelled plankton in the water.
setup.caption: 1. Put one black seed in each of 30 squares. Each square is a plankton.

setup.art: A child's hands moving five seeds from five squares into one small bowl, with six small bowls in a row.
setup.caption: 2. A small fish eats five plankton. Move the five seeds into one bowl.

setup.art: Three small bowls being tipped into a larger bowl, and two larger bowls then tipped onto a plate.
setup.caption: 3. A big fish eats three small fish. A person eats two big fish.

flow.do: Draw a grid of 30 squares on paper. Put one black seed in each square. Say that each square is one tiny plankton. Each seed is a tiny bit of pollution that the plankton took from the water. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Here are thirty tiny plankton, and each one carries a very small bit of pollution. A small fish eats five plankton. A big fish eats three small fish. A person eats two big fish. Who will have the most pollution in their body? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each square is a plankton. Each seed is a bit of pollution. Who ends up with the most? Why?

ask.q: Who do you think will have the most pollution in their body? Why?
good: The person, because they eat the most fish.
The big fish.
They will all have the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pass-It-On Seeds. You guess before you play.

flow.do: Line up six small bowls. Each bowl is a small fish. Move the seeds from five squares into each bowl. Count the seeds in one bowl and write the number.
flow.say: Six small fish. Each eats five plankton. Move the seeds from five squares into one bowl. Do it six times. How many seeds does one small fish hold?
flow.kid: Six small fish bowls. Move five seeds into each. How many seeds in one bowl?
flow.parent: Each small fish bowl holds 5 seeds. In real life, a small fish eats thousands of plankton, so the numbers are far larger. The seeds are only a way to see how it works.
flow.context: In this step, small fish eat the plankton and keep the pollution they carry.

flow.do: Take two larger bowls. Each is a big fish. Tip three small fish bowls into each big fish bowl. Count the seeds in one big fish bowl and write the number.
flow.say: Two big fish. Each eats three small fish. Tip three small bowls into each big bowl. How many seeds does one big fish hold?
flow.kid: Two big fish bowls. Tip three small bowls into each. How many seeds?
flow.parent: Each big fish bowl holds 15 seeds. The big fish cannot get rid of the pollution, so the pollution stays and adds up.

check.q: A big fish eats three small fish, and each small fish holds 5 seeds. How many seeds will the big fish hold?
options: 15 seeds
5 seeds
8 seeds
check.why: Three small fish with 5 seeds each is 3 times 5, which is 15. The big fish keeps all of it, so the big fish holds 15 seeds.

flow.context: In this step, big fish eat small fish and keep all the pollution they carry.

flow.do: First ask your child to guess how many seeds will be on the plate. Then tip both big fish bowls onto the plate and count. Write the number. Work out how many times more it is than one plankton square.
flow.say: A person eats two big fish. Tip both bowls onto the plate. How many seeds are there now? How many times more than in one plankton square?
flow.kid: Tip both big bowls onto the plate. Count the seeds. How many times more than one square?
flow.parent: The plate holds 30 seeds, which is 30 times as many as in one plankton square. In the real world, the pollutant in the water may be too thin to measure, and the fish at the top can still carry thousands of times more. With 2 to 4 children, each takes a role: plankton keeper, small fish, big fish and person. Hand the seeds on in turn. Use black peppercorns or any dry bean, and count into a dish so seeds do not roll away.
flow.context: In this step, a person eats the two big fish. You count how much pollution has built up.

flow.do: Ask what would change if the fish could pass the pollution out of their bodies. Ask what a person could do to take in less.
flow.say: What would change if the fish could get rid of the pollution? Why is it a problem when the pollution is not broken down?
flow.kid: What if fish could get rid of the pollution? What changes?
flow.parent: Pollution builds up when a body takes it in faster than it can get rid of it. Mercury leaves a body very slowly, so it adds up over a whole life. In this game every seed stays. Real animals do pass out some pollutants, and some pollutants go much faster than others.
flow.think: Which would hold more pollution, a small fish or a big fish? Which would you eat more often?
flow.context: This is the last step of Pass-It-On Seeds. You think about what makes the pollution build up.

activities.title: Ask About the Pipe: where does our used water go?

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a grown-up who knows the building or the street, such as a caretaker, a neighbour or a resident association member

activities.safety: Never open a manhole or a tank cover. Stay out of any plant room unless the caretaker takes you in. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Ask the four questions. Walk round the building and look for pipes, covers and signs.
Draw the path of the used water from your kitchen and toilet to where it ends.

activities.record: Draw a picture or map of the path, from your kitchen and toilet to where the water ends up. Write one thing you still wonder about.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out where the used water from your home goes, and whether anyone cleans it before it reaches a river, a lake or the ground.

setup.art: A child asking a caretaker questions beside a building wall with drainpipes, with a notebook open in the child's hand.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a grown-up where the used water of your building goes.

setup.art: A child looking at a manhole cover and a green sign on a small plant room door from a safe distance.
setup.caption: 2. Look for covers, pipes and signs. Do not open anything.

setup.art: A simple drawn map with arrows from a kitchen and a toilet, through a treatment tank, to a river.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the path of the used water on paper.

flow.do: Ask a grown-up these four questions. Where does the water from our toilets and kitchens go? Is there a treatment plant, a septic tank or a sewer? Who looks after it? What happens to the cleaned water? Write the answers.
flow.say: Let us ask the caretaker four questions. Where does our used water go? Is it cleaned? Who looks after it? What happens to the clean water afterwards?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up where our used water goes. Is it cleaned? Who looks after it?

ask.q: Where do you think our used water goes?
good: Into the river.
Into the ground.
To a plant that cleans it.

flow.parent: Many large apartment blocks in Indian cities have a small treatment plant, and use the clean water for gardens and flushing. Other homes are linked to a sewer pipe under the road, or to a septic tank. In some places the drain ends in a stormwater drain or a nala. Write the answer you get, even if it is 'I do not know'. If you live in a house in a village or small town, ask a neighbour, the panchayat or ward office, or the mason who built the house. Many homes use a septic tank and a soak pit. With 2 to 4 children, each child asks one of the four questions and writes the answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask About the Pipe. You ask where the used water goes.

flow.do: Walk round the building with the grown-up. Look for drain pipes, covers with writing, a small plant room, and signs. Draw what you see. Do not open any cover or tank.
flow.say: Walk round the building and look for pipes, covers and signs. Draw what you find. We do not open anything.
flow.kid: Look for pipes, covers and signs. Draw them. Do not open anything.
flow.parent: A plant room may have a sign such as STP. That stands for sewage treatment plant. You can ask the caretaker to show it from the door. Do not go in unless you are taken in.

check.q: Why do we not open covers or tanks?
options: They may hold harmful gases and germs, and it is not safe to lean over them
They are always empty
It would take too long
check.why: Tanks and manholes can hold gases that cannot be seen or smelled and that can harm. Germs from sewage are there too. Looking from outside is safe, and opening is a job for trained people.

flow.context: In this step, you look for the signs of where the water goes.

flow.do: On day two, draw the path on a sheet of paper. Start at your kitchen tap and your toilet. Follow it with arrows to wherever it ends. Mark the stages where it is cleaned, and the stage where it is not. Write one thing you still wonder about.
flow.say: Draw the path of your used water, with arrows. Start at your kitchen and toilet. Where does it end? Is it cleaned on the way? What do you still wonder about?
flow.kid: Draw the path of your used water. Where does it end? Is it cleaned?
flow.parent: If your building has no treatment, this is a good thing to talk about as a family or as a building. If there is a plant, ask who checks the water that leaves it, and how often.
flow.think: When your water goes out of the building, where is 'away'?
flow.context: This is the last step of Ask About the Pipe. You draw the path and say what you wonder about.

activities.title: Our Nearest Water: what is it used for, and what does it carry?

materials.item: a phone or computer with a map
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: If you go to see the water, a grown-up comes too. Keep well back from the edge, and do not touch the water.
activities.record: Write the name of the water, what it is used for, and one thing it may carry. Write how its water is checked, or write that you could not find out.
activities.context: In this activity, you find the river, lake or pond nearest to your home and find out how it is checked. You ask what it is clean for.

setup.art: A map on a phone screen with a blue river passing near a town, with a pin on the nearest bend.
setup.caption: 1. Find the nearest river, lake or pond on a map.

setup.art: A web page of a pollution control board with a table of water quality results and a highlighted row.
setup.caption: 2. Look for a water quality report. Find out how the water is checked.

setup.art: A child's notebook page with the name of a river, three used-for icons (bathing, fishing, washing) and a question mark.
setup.caption: 3. Write what the water is used for and what it may carry.

flow.do: Open a map on a phone. Find the nearest river, lake, canal or pond. Write its name. Ask where its water comes from and where it goes.
flow.say: Let us find the water nearest to our home. What is its name? Where does its water come from? Where does it go?
flow.kid: Find the nearest river, lake or pond on a map. What is it called?

ask.q: What do people use this water for?
good: Washing clothes.
Bathing.
Fishing.
Farming.
Drinking.

flow.parent: Zoom in until you can see where the water comes from. In a city, the nearest water may be a lake or a canal. If you cannot find one, use the biggest river in your state.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Nearest Water. You find the water nearest to your home.

flow.do: Search for the water's name with the words water quality, and add the pollution control board of your state. Look for a table, a news story or a report. Write one number or fact, or write that you could not find one.
flow.say: Search for your water's name and the words water quality. What do you find? Is there a table or a report? Write one fact, or write that there is nothing to find.
flow.kid: Search for the water's name and water quality. Write one fact you find.
flow.parent: Rivers in India are given a best-use class from A to E by the Central Pollution Control Board. Class A is drinking water after disinfection and Class B is outdoor bathing. Class E is only for irrigation and cooling. The reports are on the board's website at cpcb.nic.in. Many local waters have no report, and that is itself something to note. The data may be hard to read, so help your child find one fact. With 2 to 4 children, one searches, one reads the result aloud, and one writes the fact.
flow.context: In this step, you look for how the water is checked, and what the checks found.

flow.do: Ask your child to write what this water is used for and what it is clean enough for. Ask what it may carry that cannot be seen.
flow.say: What is this water used for? Is it clean enough for that? What could it carry that we cannot see?
flow.kid: What is this water used for? Is it clean enough for that?
flow.parent: There is no single right answer. The point is that 'clean' depends on the use. Water that is fine for washing a scooter may not be fine for drinking, and water for drinking after treatment may not be fine for a baby's bath.
flow.think: A river can be fine for irrigating fields and not for drinking. Is it clean, or not clean?
flow.context: This is the last step of Our Nearest Water. You ask what the water is clean for.

projects.title: Clay, Colour and the Bucket: what happens to a festival figure in water?

materials.item: potter's clay or art clay, about 3 lumps the size of a lemon (from a potter or an art shop, about Rs 30 to 60 a kilo)
turmeric powder and kumkum (or a little beetroot juice for the red), with a few drops of water to make paste
a little water-based poster paint, red or yellow, and a brush
3 buckets or large bowls, and 3 litres of water
newspaper, a tray and a marker pen
a clear jar for looking at the water

projects.safety: Use only water-based paint that says non-toxic on the label, and a kumkum you know is safe for skin. Wash hands after handling clay and paint. Do not put paint water on plants or down the drain: an adult will decide where it goes. Keep paint away from mouths. Check that nobody is allergic to turmeric or the paint, and wear old clothes, because turmeric stains.

schedule.what: Shape three small figures or diyas from clay. Paint one with turmeric and kumkum paste, and one with poster paint. Leave the third plain.
Turn the figures over so that they dry on all sides. Leave them until they are hard and pale, 2 to 3 days, or longer in damp weather.
Put each figure in its own bucket of water. Watch and write what happens every ten minutes for half an hour.
Look at the buckets. Let the mud settle and look at the water. Decide where each bucket's water should go.

projects.record: Draw the three figures and the three buckets on day 3 and day 4. Write what happened to each figure, and what colour the water was.
projects.context: In this project, you test what happens to a clay figure and two kinds of colour when they are put in water, as at a festival. You see what comes out of the clay and the colour, and what stays in the water.

setup.art: Three small clay figures on a tray: one plain, one painted with yellow and red paste, and one painted with bright poster paint.
setup.caption: 1. Make three small clay figures. Leave one plain. Paint one with turmeric and kumkum paste and one with poster paint.

setup.art: Three buckets of water with a figure sitting in each, and a clock showing ten minutes between pictures.
setup.caption: 2. After two days of drying, put each figure in its own bucket. Look every ten minutes.

setup.art: Three jars of water side by side next morning, with mud settled at the bottom of each, one yellowish, one pinkish and one clear.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, look at the water in each bucket. What settled, and what is still in the water?

flow.do: Show the materials. Explain that at some festivals, people dip clay figures in water. Ask what will happen to each figure and to the water. Write down your child's guess and the reason.
flow.say: At some festivals, a clay figure is dipped in water at the end. We will test three figures: plain clay, clay with turmeric and kumkum, and clay with poster paint. What will happen to each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will dip three clay figures in water. What will happen to each? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the water?
good: It will turn brown.
The colour will come off into the water.
The clay will sink to the bottom.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many local pollution control boards ask people to use natural clay figures and natural colours at festivals. Plaster of Paris figures stay hard in water for a very long time. This project tests clay.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clay, Colour and the Bucket project. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Shape three equal lumps into small figures or diyas. Press them firmly so there are no cracks. Paint figure 2 with turmeric and kumkum paste. Paint figure 3 with a thin layer of poster paint. Leave figure 1 plain. Put them on newspaper in a dry place.
flow.say: Shape three lumps of clay into small figures, all the same size. Paint figure 2 with turmeric and kumkum paste. Paint figure 3 with poster paint. Leave figure 1 plain. Set them in a dry place.
flow.kid: Shape three clay figures. Paint two. Leave one plain. Let them dry.
flow.context: In this step, you make the three figures and colour them.

flow.do: Turn the figures over on day two so that they dry on every side. Check that no figure has cracked. Keep drying until the clay is hard. This takes 2 to 3 days, or longer in monsoon weather.
flow.say: Turn the figures over today so that they dry all round.
flow.kid: Turn the figures over. Let them dry.
flow.context: In this step, you let the clay dry for a second day.

flow.do: Pour 1 litre of water into each bucket. Gently place a figure in each. Every ten minutes, look at each bucket and write what you see. Do this for thirty minutes. Do not stir the water.
flow.say: Pour one litre of water into each bucket. Lower a figure into each one gently. Every ten minutes, look at each bucket and write what has happened.
flow.kid: Put one figure in each bucket. Look every ten minutes. Write what you see.

ask.q: What do you see coming off each figure?
good: Brown cloud from the clay.
Yellow or red colour from the paste.
Flakes from the paint.

flow.parent: Unfired clay softens at its surface within the first hour, and its water goes cloudy. The turmeric and kumkum colour spreads into the water. Poster paint may colour the water too, and flakes of paint may float or sink. Results vary with the clay. With 2 to 4 children, each child shapes, paints and watches one figure, and any extra child keeps the clock and the notebook. If you have fewer than three children, one child can do all three. Small figures dry faster and fall apart faster than big ones.
flow.context: In this step, you watch what happens when each figure sits in water.

flow.do: The next morning, look at each bucket from the side. Pour a little water from each into a clear jar to see it better. Write what has settled to the bottom and what colour the water is. Decide where the water should go.
flow.say: Look at each bucket the next morning. What has settled at the bottom? Is the water still coloured? Pour a little into a jar to look closely.
flow.kid: Look at each bucket. What settled at the bottom? Is the water still coloured?
flow.parent: The clay settles, but some of the colour stays in the water. Turmeric is only partly dissolved, so the water may be yellow and slightly cloudy. The water from the plain clay and the natural colours can go on garden soil or a plant pot, far from edible plants. Keep the poster paint water out of soil and away from plants. Ask an adult to pour it into the toilet, or save it for another painting.
flow.think: Mud settled at the bottom, but the colour is still in the water. Why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Clay, Colour and the Bucket project. You see what stays in the water.

challenges.title: The Spill Boom: keep the oil in one corner
challenges.safety: Oil on the floor is slippery, so work on a tray over newspaper. Cut the card and foil with an adult's help. Never pour oily water down the sink.
challenges.problem: A boat has spilled oil in a harbour. Waves are pushing it towards the beach. Make a floating barrier, called a boom, that keeps the oil in one corner of a tray of water while the waves roll.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Use cooking oil only, one tablespoon at a time.
Work over a tray and old newspaper.
The boom must float on its own, and the waves must be made by gently rocking the tray.
materials: a large shallow tray or baking dish
general: A ring of straws taped end to end, floating on the water around the oil.
A rolled paper towel or a row of corks tied with string, floating around the oil.
A line of bottle caps taped together in a ring.
creative: Add a skirt of foil or card hanging under the ring, because oil can creep under a boom that has no skirt.
Use two rings, one inside the other, in case the first leaks.
Stuff a clean stocking with hair or cotton wool to make a boom that also soaks up oil.
challenges.your_turn: Add 3 tablespoons of oil and rock the tray harder. Take off one feature at a time, such as the skirt, and test again. Which feature mattered most?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about oil spills. You make and test a floating boom that holds oil in one place so it can be cleared up.

setup.art: A tray of water with a golden patch of oil in the middle and a ring of straws floating around it.
setup.caption: 1. Float a ring of straws around the oil.

setup.art: The same tray tilting gently, with the oil escaping under the ring and out to one side.
setup.caption: 2. Rock the tray. Does the oil stay inside the ring? Count the seconds.

setup.art: A better ring with a foil skirt hanging underneath it in the water, and the oil staying inside.
setup.caption: 3. Add a skirt that hangs underneath, and test again.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask how the oil will spread, and what could stop it. Put 1 litre of water in the tray and 1 tablespoon of oil in the middle.
flow.say: Oil from a spill spreads out on the water. We need a barrier that floats and keeps the oil inside. How could you make one with what we have?
flow.kid: Oil spreads on water. How could we make a floating ring to hold it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spill Boom challenge. You think about what could keep the oil in.

flow.do: Make a ring from straws and tape. Float it around the oil. Rock the tray gently for thirty seconds. Count how many seconds the oil stays inside. Write the number.
flow.say: Make a ring from straws and tape. Float it around the oil. Rock the tray gently. How long does the oil stay inside?
flow.kid: Make a straw ring. Float it round the oil. Rock the tray. Count the seconds.
flow.parent: The oil usually slips under the straws or flows over them as the water rocks. That tells you what the boom needs.
flow.context: In this step, you make the first boom and test it.

flow.do: Add a skirt, a strip of foil or card that hangs down into the water from the ring. Test again for the same time. Try another idea, such as a double ring. Write the seconds for each.
flow.say: Now add a skirt, a strip of foil that hangs down into the water. Test again. Does the oil stay inside longer?
flow.kid: Add a skirt of foil to the ring. Rock the tray. Does the oil stay in longer?

check.q: Why does a real boom have a skirt that hangs under the water?
options: Oil can slip under a barrier that only floats on top
To make the boom look bigger
To hold the boom in place with sand
check.why: Oil floats on the surface, but moving water pushes it down and under a shallow barrier. A skirt reaches below the surface, so the oil cannot slip underneath.

flow.context: In this step, you improve the boom and test it again.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose their best boom and say why it works. Then ask what one change they would try next. Scoop the oil into the container and wipe up with paper.
flow.say: Which boom was best? Why did it work? What would you change next?
flow.kid: Which boom was best? Why? What would you change?
flow.parent: A boom only holds the oil in place, so that boats and pads can then remove it. Pour the oily water into a container and put it out with the dry waste. Do not pour it down the sink.
flow.think: A boom keeps oil in one place. Does it take the oil out of the water?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Spill Boom challenge. You say which boom worked best and why.
