quiz.p: Sneha stirs one spoonful of red water into a full tumbler of clean water and stirs it well. What is true about the red stuff?
opts: It is all still there, spread through more water
Half of it disappears
It all disappears
quiz.why: Mixing spreads the red stuff out, but it does not destroy it. The strength falls and the amount stays the same.

quiz.p: A cup of water looks exactly like tap water, but a nose can pick it out. What is the best explanation?
opts: Something is in the water that the eye cannot see but the nose can find
The nose is always more correct than the eye
The cup is empty
quiz.why: Both senses check different things. The nose found something in the water that was too thin for the eye to see.

quiz.p: Which tool could lift a floating plastic bag off a pond?
opts: A net
A cloth
A tumbler
quiz.why: A plastic bag floats and is big, so a net can lift it out.

quiz.p: Salty water is poured through a thick cloth. Why does it come out just as salty?
opts: Dissolved salt is in single tiny pieces that pass through the gaps
The cloth adds salt
Salt cannot be seen
quiz.why: The gaps in a cloth are much bigger than the pieces of dissolved salt. So the salt goes through with the water.

quiz.p: Farhan sniffs three cups with one scented cup, and points to the right one three times in a row. What is the best conclusion?
opts: He probably smelled it, because guessing would rarely give three in a row
He must have looked
It proves he has a very good nose
quiz.why: Guessing right three times in a row happens only 1 time in 27. So it is likely he smelled it, though one test cannot prove more than that.

quiz.p: Why can too much kitchen waste in a pond kill fish?
opts: Microbes eating the waste use up the oxygen
The waste is a poison
The waste makes the water too hot
quiz.why: Microbes that eat the waste breathe in the oxygen dissolved in the water. If it runs low, fish cannot breathe.

quiz.p: Fertiliser washes from a field into a pond. What happens to the algae in the pond?
opts: They grow thickly, because the fertiliser is food for them
They die, because fertiliser is poison for them
Nothing changes
quiz.why: Fertiliser holds nitrogen and phosphorus, which feed plants and algae. Algae can then cover the pond.

quiz.p: A river holds a tiny trace of mercury. Plankton, small fish, big fish and a heron live there. Which one holds the most mercury?
opts: The heron
The plankton
They all hold the same
quiz.why: Mercury is kept in the body and passed up the food chain. The heron at the top eats the most fish, so she holds the most.

quiz.p: What does the settling tank in a sewage plant do?
opts: Lets heavy bits sink to the bottom as sludge
Kills the germs
Lets microbes breathe
quiz.why: The water stands still, and heavy bits sink. Killing germs happens in a later stage.

quiz.p: Boiling water kills the germs in it.
quiz.why: True. Heat kills most germs. But boiling does not take out dissolved chemicals.

quiz.p: River A is marked 'best for outdoor bathing' and river B is marked 'best for drinking after treatment'. What does this show?
opts: Clean always means clean for a use
River B is dirtier
Rivers cannot be tested
quiz.why: Each use has its own tests and limits. So the same water can pass for one use and fail for another.

quiz.p: A well's water looks clear and smells fine. How can you tell whether it is safe to drink?
opts: Have it tested for the things that matter
Taste a big sip
Look at it again in the sun
quiz.why: Looking, smelling and tasting find only some things. A lab can measure the others.

items.p: You stir one spoonful of red water into a full tumbler of clean water. What has happened to the amount of red stuff?
opts: It is all still there, spread through more water
Half of it has disappeared
It has all gone
items.why: Mixing spreads the red stuff through more water, so each sip is paler. But nothing is destroyed when things mix. The amount stays the same, and only the strength falls.

items.p: After four steps of thinning, the colour is too faint to see. Which sentence is right?
opts: The colour is gone for good
The colour is still there, but too thin for our eyes
The water has made new colour
items.why: Each step spread the colour through more water. The colour was too thin to show up to the eye, but it was still in the water, and a nose or an instrument may find what an eye cannot.

items.p: If water looks clear, there is nothing in it.
items.why: False. Salt, dye, petrol, germs and many chemicals can be in clear water. Looking is only one way of checking.

items.p: In the tumbler test, each step made the mix about ____ times weaker.
a: forty-one
forty one
items.why: A spoonful of 5 millilitres ended up in 205 millilitres of water. 205 divided by 5 is 41.

items.p: Match each kind of dirt in water to the tool that can take it out.
pairs: Mud that has stirred up in still water
letting it settle, then a cloth
none of the simple tools: it needs special filters or evaporation
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Things that float can be lifted out. Things that sink settle, and a cloth catches the rest. Dissolved things are too small for any net or cloth.

items.p: Sort each thing by how it behaves in water.
items.a: as given
items.why: Light things float and heavy grains sink. Salt and sugar break into single tiny pieces and spread through the water.

items.p: A thick cloth is held over a glass and salty water is poured through it. Is the water in the glass still salty?
opts: Yes, because salt is dissolved in single tiny pieces that pass through
No, because the cloth catches salt
No, because cloth turns salt into water
items.why: A cloth has gaps that are far wider than a single piece of dissolved salt. So the salt goes through with the water. A cloth can only catch bits that are bigger than its gaps.

items.p: A child sniffs three cups, with only one scented, and just guesses each time. She does 30 trials. About how many will she get right by luck alone?
items.why: With three cups, a guess is right one time in three. One third of 30 is 10. If she gets many more right than 10, she is not just guessing.

items.p: Put these steps of a fair blind sniff test in order.
a: Pour plain water in two cups and scented water in one
Roll a die to decide where the odd cup goes
The child shuts their eyes and sniffs all three
The child points, and the grown-up writes right or wrong
Repeat the test three times
items.why: The die stops the grown-up from choosing the place by habit. Shut eyes stop the child from seeing a difference. Repeating the test shows whether the result was luck.

items.p: In a fair blind test, the person who sniffs may look at the cups first.
items.why: False. If the person can look, they might see a difference, such as a trace of colour or the way the cups are placed. Shut eyes make sure only the nose is being tested.

items.p: A friend says: 'The river near our house looks clear, so it must be clean.' What would you tell your friend, using what you know about water?
items.a: Looking only checks for things the eye can see. Dissolved things like dye, chemicals and some germs can be in clear water. Colour can also get too thin to see. To know if water is clean, it must be tested for the things we care about, and clean also depends on what it is for.
items.why: A strong answer says that clear does not mean clean, names something that hides in clear water, and says that testing is needed.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a pond with too much waste in it. Label the three parts: the thick green layer, the crowd of tiny living beings feeding on waste, and the fish gasping.
labels: Thick green layer on the surface
Tiny living beings around floating waste
Fish near the surface with open mouths
items.art: A pond at dawn with a thick green layer of algae on the surface, bacteria crowded around floating waste in a magnified circle, and fish at the surface with open mouths.
a: Thick green layer on the surface: algae
Tiny living beings around floating waste: bacteria
Fish near the surface with open mouths: fish gasping for oxygen
items.why: Plant food grows the algae. When the waste and dead algae feed bacteria, the bacteria use up the oxygen, and the fish go up to find air.

items.p: Why do fish gasp at the surface of a pond that has a lot of rotting waste in it?
opts: The microbes eating the waste have used up the oxygen in the water
The waste is poisonous gas
The fish want to eat the waste
items.why: Microbes eating the waste breathe in oxygen, so there is less left for the fish. At the surface a little oxygen comes in from the air.

items.p: Draw a food chain with plankton, a small fish, a big fish and a heron. Show a little pollution in the plankton, and draw how much builds up in each animal after that.
items.a: Four animals in a row, with a few dots in the plankton and more and more dots in each one that comes after, ending with the most in the heron.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the dots growing along the chain, because each animal keeps the pollution of everything they eat.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Salt, sugar, mud, dye. Think about which can be caught by a cloth.
items.a: Mud. Salt, sugar and dye all dissolve in water and pass through a cloth. Mud does not dissolve, and a cloth can catch it.
items.why: Dissolved things are too small to be caught. Mud grains are bigger than the gaps in a cloth, so it is held back.

items.p: A factory lets its treated waste water into a big river. Its manager says the river is so big that it will thin out any waste.

views.says: The river is huge. Our water is treated, and it thins out quickly. There is nothing to worry about.
I cannot see anything in the water. But my catch has got smaller every year, and the fish taste different.
We cannot tell by looking. Take water samples above and below the pipe and measure. And check the fish too.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and says what measurement would help, such as testing the water above and below the pipe, or testing the fish.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer weighs the claim and asks for evidence, rather than trusting what the water looks like.

items.p: A river is marked 'best for outdoor bathing'. What does that tell you about drinking it straight from the river?
opts: Nothing: bathing water can still need cleaning before it is safe to drink
It is also safe to drink
It is not safe to bathe in
items.why: Each use has its own tests and limits. Water can be fine for bathing and still need treatment before drinking. 'Clean' means clean for a use.

items.p: A heavy shower washes leaves, fertiliser and cow dung into a village pond. A week later the pond is thick and green. What happened first?
opts: The plant food in the runoff made algae grow thickly
The cow dung turned into algae
The rain made the water green
items.why: Fertiliser and dung carry nitrogen and phosphorus, which feed algae. The algae multiply quickly and turn the pond green.

items.p: In a pond with a thick algal bloom, the oxygen can be lowest just before dawn.
items.why: True. At night the algae and the microbes use oxygen and no sunlight is making more. By dawn there can be very little left for the fish.

items.p: When a pollutant that is not broken down builds up inside living bodies, it is called bio____.
a: accumulation
bioaccumulation
items.why: Accumulation means piling up. The pollutant is taken in faster than the body can get rid of it, so it adds up.

items.p: Health warnings tell some people to eat large sea fish, such as shark, less often than small fish. What is the reason?
opts: Large fish eat many fish and so keep more of the mercury in them
Large fish taste bad
Small fish have no mercury at all
items.why: Mercury is not passed out of a body quickly. A large fish eats many smaller fish over many years and keeps what is in them, so it holds the most.

items.p: A plankton holds 1 unit of a pollutant. A small fish eats 20 plankton. A big fish eats 10 small fish. How many units does the big fish hold, if nothing is passed out?
items.why: A small fish holds 20 units. A big fish eats 10 of them, so the big fish holds 10 times 20, which is 200 units.

items.p: Match each stage of a sewage treatment plant to what it takes out.
pairs: heavy bits that sink as sludge
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each stage takes out a different kind of dirt. Screens catch big things, settling takes the heavy bits, microbes eat the waste that is dissolved or very fine, and the last stage kills germs.

items.p: Put the stages of a sewage treatment plant in order.
a: Screens catch rags and plastic
Heavy bits settle as sludge
Air and microbes eat the waste
Chlorine or ultraviolet light kills germs
items.why: Big things come out first so they do not block anything. Then the heavy bits settle. Microbes do most of the cleaning, and the germs are killed last.

items.p: In the third stage of a sewage plant, air is bubbled through the tank. Why?
opts: The microbes that clean the water need oxygen to breathe
The air makes the water colder
The air pushes the sludge out
items.why: The microbes that eat the waste breathe oxygen. Without bubbles, the oxygen would run out and they could not do the cleaning.

items.p: Sort each method by whether it takes out bits or kills germs.
items.a: as given
items.why: Nets, cloths and settling catch things that are big enough to hold back. Heat, chlorine and ultraviolet light harm germs, which are alive.

items.p: Boiling water takes out dissolved pesticides.
items.why: False. Boiling kills germs, but dissolved chemicals stay in the water. As water boils away, the chemicals left behind get stronger.

items.p: A torch beam shows up in water with a drop of milk, but not in water with dissolved salt. Explain why.
items.a: Milk is made of tiny floating bits that scatter the light, so the beam shows. Dissolved salt is in single tiny pieces that scatter almost no light, so the beam is not seen. A torch can find floating bits but not dissolved things.
items.why: A strong answer says that the light bounces off floating bits, that dissolved things are too small to do this, and that the torch is another check that misses some things.

items.p: A factory pours a litre of dye into a big river. A kilometre downstream the water looks clear. Is the dye gone? Explain.
items.a: No. The dye has been spread through more water, so it is too thin to see, but it has not been destroyed. The amount is the same. Some of it may settle in mud, be taken in by living things, or flow on to the sea.
items.why: A strong answer says that thinning lowers the strength but not the amount, and says where the dye might be now.

items.p: Draw a floating oil boom around a spill. Show the part above the water, the skirt under the water and the oil inside.
items.a: A ring on the water with a float above the surface and a skirt hanging down below it, and oil inside the ring.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the skirt reaching below the surface, since oil can slip under a barrier that only floats on top.

items.p: A town wants to let its treated sewage into a big lake. It says the lake will mix and thin the water.

views.says: The sewage is treated, and the lake is huge. Building a better plant would cost too much.
Fish need oxygen. If the water has too much waste, the oxygen goes, and my family's living goes with it.
It depends on what is left in the water. Measure the oxygen, the nutrients and the germs. Then decide.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What would you want to measure first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and names a measurement such as dissolved oxygen, nutrients or germs.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer asks for measurements before deciding, and thinks about those who live in the lake.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Lead, mercury, banana peel, arsenic.
items.a: Banana peel. The others are elements, which nothing alive can break down. A banana peel is eaten by microbes and rots away.
items.why: Lead, mercury and arsenic are elements. They can move or be locked away, but they stay what they are. Microbes can digest a banana peel.

items.p: Which waste would use up the most oxygen in a pond?
opts: A bucket of leftover dal and rice
A bucket of clean sand
A bucket of small stones
items.why: Dal and rice are food for microbes. As the microbes eat it, they breathe in the oxygen. Sand and stones are not food, so they use none.

items.p: A lab tests your well and finds nothing wrong. Your nose still smells petrol. What would you do next, and why?
items.a: Test again with a different lab or a different test for petrol. Take a fresh sample in a clean glass bottle and keep it cold. Tell the village leader. A test only finds what it is looking for, so a test for one thing can miss another.
items.why: A strong answer treats the nose as a reason to test more, and says that each test checks only certain things.

items.p: What is the best reason to measure water with an instrument, as well as looking and smelling?
opts: A measurement gives a number that different people can compare
Instruments are always right
Looking never finds anything
items.why: Eyes and noses differ from person to person. A number from a good instrument can be compared by anyone, and checked against a safe limit.

items.p: A water test that finds no germs proves that the water has no chemicals in it.
items.why: False. A germ test finds signs of germs only. Chemicals need their own tests.

items.p: Match each check to what it can find.
pairs: mud and colour in a thick layer
some smells at very low amounts
how much air the fish have
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each check sees one part of the water. None of them sees all of it.

items.p: After an oil spill at sea, some agencies spray dispersants, chemicals that break the oil into tiny droplets.

views.says: Dispersants keep oil from reaching the beach and the birds. The droplets are then eaten by microbes.
The oil is still in the water, and now it is in droplets that fish and corals can take in. We need more studies of the harm.

views.who: A fisherwoman on the coast (an imagined view)
views.says: If the spray keeps the beach clean but poisons my fish, who has it helped?

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What would you want to find out first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason and names evidence, such as how the droplets affect fish, or how fast microbes eat them.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer weighs both the clean beach and the harm in the water.

items.p: The East Kolkata Wetlands clean a city's sewage in shallow fish ponds. Name two kinds of living beings that help, and say what each one does.
items.a: Microbes eat the waste in the water and use oxygen. Algae grow on the nutrients and give out oxygen in the sunlight. Fish eat the algae and other small creatures, and are taken to market. Plants and reeds also take up nutrients.
items.why: A strong answer names two living things and links what each one does to the cleaning of the water.

items.p: Why does a lake with a heavy algal bloom often lose its fish a week or two later?
opts: The dead algae feed microbes, which use up the oxygen
The algae eat the fish
The algae make the water too cold
items.why: When the algae die, microbes eat them and breathe in the oxygen. With less oxygen left, the fish cannot breathe.

items.p: Each step of a thinning test makes the mix 41 times weaker. After three steps, how many times weaker is the last tumbler than the first? Use 41 times 41 is 1,681.
items.why: After two steps the mix is 1,681 times weaker. One more step multiplies by 41 again. 1,681 times 41 is 68,921.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Plastic bag, thermocol, rice husk, salt.
items.a: Salt. It dissolves and cannot be netted. The other three float, and a net can lift them out.
items.why: Floating things can be taken out with a net. Dissolved things cannot.

items.p: Draw a river from the hills to the sea. Mark one point source of pollution with a P and one place where runoff comes in with an R.

items.why: A strong drawing shows a point source as one pipe or drain, and runoff as many streams across the land.

items.p: If the sea has a little mercury, which fish should people eat less often: a tiny sardine, or a large shark?
opts: A large shark, because it has eaten many fish and kept their mercury
A tiny sardine, because it is smaller
Both hold the same amount
items.why: Mercury builds up along a food chain. A large fish at the top holds far more than a small one near the bottom.

items.p: A fish in water that has only a tiny amount of mercury can still hold a lot of it in its body.
items.why: True. A fish takes in a little with every meal and cannot get rid of it quickly, so over her life it adds up.

items.p: Fish in a polluted pond gasp at the surface because the water has too little dissolved ____.
a: oxygen
items.why: Fish breathe the oxygen that is dissolved in water. Microbes eating waste can use it up.

items.p: Put the response to an oil spill in the best order.
a: Float a boom round the spill
Skim or soak up the oil
Clean the shore and check the water
items.why: A boom first, so the oil stops spreading. The thicker the oil, the easier it is to remove. Cleaning the shore and checking the water comes last.

items.p: Here is a drawing of an oil boom. Label the three parts: the float above the water, the skirt below the water and the oil.
labels: The part that sits above the water
The strip that hangs below the water
The layer on the water inside the ring
items.art: A cut-away of a boom in water with a round float above the surface, a skirt hanging down, and a golden layer of oil inside.
a: The part that sits above the water: the float
The strip that hangs below the water: the skirt
The layer on the water inside the ring: the oil
items.why: The float keeps the boom on the surface, and the skirt stops oil slipping underneath.

items.p: Write a short notice for your building or village that says why 'it looks clear' is not enough to say that water is safe.
items.a: Water that looks clear can still carry things we cannot see, such as dissolved chemicals and germs. Our eyes lose a colour before our nose loses a smell, and an instrument finds even less. So water must be tested for the things that matter, and tested again from time to time.
items.why: A strong answer says clear does not mean clean, gives one example of something hidden, and asks for testing.

items.p: Kavya gets 2 of 3 trials right in a three-cup sniff test. What is the best conclusion?
opts: It could easily be luck, so repeat with more trials
She definitely smelled it
She definitely did not smell it
items.why: Getting 2 or more of 3 right by pure guessing happens about 1 time in 4. A better test has more trials.

applications: Water-supply boards and village panchayats test wells and taps for germs, chemicals and oxygen, rather than trusting how the water looks.
Sewage treatment plants in apartment blocks and towns clean used water so it can be reused for gardens or flushing.
Pollution control boards give rivers a best-use class, and check whether each stretch is clean enough for its use.
Floating booms and skimmers hold and clear oil after a ship accident.
Factories have effluent treatment plants that clean their waste water before it leaves.
Health warnings about mercury in large fish, such as shark and swordfish.
Farmers who use less fertiliser, or spread it in the right amount and at the right time, keep it from washing into ponds and rivers.
Scientists use mussels and oysters as living collectors, because they filter lots of water and keep what they cannot break down.
Clay idols and natural colours at festivals, so that less paint and plaster go into lakes and rivers.
Citizens who test their local pond or lake and share the results, so that the people in charge can see the problem.

open_questions.q: What do microplastics do to a body over a whole lifetime?
open_questions.why_open: They have been found in blood and in many organs, but it takes many years and many people to find out what harm they do. The studies so far are early.

open_questions.q: Can microbes be found or made that eat plastic fast enough to help clean the world?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016, Japanese scientists reported a bacterium that digests one common plastic, PET, but very slowly. Whether this can be made fast and safe at a large scale is not known.

open_questions.q: Is there any amount of a harmful chemical in water that is completely safe?
open_questions.why_open: For some chemicals, harm has been found even at low amounts. For others, scientists have not found a level below which there is no harm at all.

open_questions.q: How much can a river take before she can no longer clean herself?
open_questions.why_open: Each river is different. It depends on her flow, her temperature, her microbes and the season, and measuring all of it is hard.

open_questions.q: How do dispersants change the long-term harm of an oil spill?
open_questions.why_open: Studies after big spills disagree. Some find that oil breaks down faster. Others find that fish and corals take in more of it.

open_questions.q: How should we measure the health of a river: by chemicals, or by the fish, birds and plants who live there too?
open_questions.why_open: Both give part of the picture. Scientists and communities still argue about which counts more, and whose measures should decide.

maths.problem: Each step in the tumbler test makes the mix 41 times weaker. How many times weaker than tumbler 1 is tumbler 3?
maths.explain: Tumbler 2 is 41 times weaker than tumbler 1. Tumbler 3 is 41 times weaker again, so it is 41 times 41. 40 times 41 is 1,640, and one more 41 makes 1,681.
maths.context: In the Gone from Sight test, each tumbler is 41 times weaker than the one before.
maths.why_maths: When a thing is made weaker by the same amount each time, you multiply the amounts together to find the total.

maths.problem: Zainab sniffs three cups and just guesses. She does three trials. How many different ways can her three guesses go, if each trial has three cups to pick from? How many of them are all right?
maths.answer: 27 ways, and only 1 of them is all right.
maths.explain: The first guess can go 3 ways, the second 3 ways and the third 3 ways. 3 times 3 times 3 is 27. Only one of the 27 has all three right. So by luck alone she gets all three right 1 time in 27.
maths.context: In the Gone from Sight test, a child sniffs three cups, and one of them has a scent.
maths.why_maths: Counting all the ways a guess can go tells you how unlikely it is to get every one right by luck.

maths.problem: A level teaspoon holds 5 millilitres. How many teaspoons of water are there in 205 millilitres?
maths.explain: 205 divided by 5 is 41. So one teaspoon is one forty-first of the mix. That is why each step made the mix 41 times weaker.
maths.context: In the Gone from Sight test, a spoonful goes into 200 millilitres of water, making 205 millilitres.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the whole by the part tells you how many times thinner the mix has become.

maths.problem: In an imagined class result, the shine left on the bowls after two minutes was: control 5, spoon 2, paper towel 3, cotton wool 2, hair 3 and dishwash liquid 1. Which tool had the lowest score? Does that mean its water was the cleanest?
maths.answer: Dishwash liquid had the lowest score, 1. It does not mean the cleanest water.
maths.explain: The bar for dishwash liquid is the shortest. But the paper strip test showed oil spots in the bowls, and dishwash liquid breaks oil into tiny drops that stay in the water. So a low shine score alone does not show clean water.
maths.context: In the Oil Spill Race, you score the shine left on each bowl after two minutes.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart lets you compare the scores at a glance, and you then ask whether a score really measures what you want.

chart.title: Shine left on each bowl after two minutes (an imagined class result)

maths.problem: In Pass-It-On Seeds, a small fish eats 5 plankton, a big fish eats 3 small fish and a person eats 2 big fish. Each plankton holds 1 seed. How many seeds does the person hold, and how many times more is that than one plankton?
maths.answer: 30 seeds, which is 30 times as many as one plankton.
maths.explain: A small fish holds 5 seeds. A big fish holds 3 times 5, which is 15. A person holds 2 times 15, which is 30. One plankton holds 1, so the person holds 30 times as much.
maths.context: In Pass-It-On Seeds, black seeds stand for pollution moving up a food chain.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying along the chain shows how fast a small amount adds up when nothing is passed out.

maths.problem: A town makes 20 million litres of sewage a day. Its plant can treat 12 million litres. This is an imagined town. What fraction of the sewage is not treated?
maths.explain: 20 million take away 12 million is 8 million litres not treated. 8 out of 20 is the same as 2 out of 5. In many Indian towns, less than half of the sewage is treated.
maths.context: Sewage plants clean used water in stages, but many towns have plants that can treat only part of their sewage.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how big the untreated part is, compared with the whole.

maths.problem: A village's well is polluted, so a tanker brings 6,000 litres of water for 900 rupees. The village uses 18,000 litres a day. What does the water cost for one day? What for 30 days?
maths.answer: 2,700 rupees a day, and 81,000 rupees for 30 days.
maths.explain: 18,000 litres is 3 tankers, because 18,000 divided by 6,000 is 3. 3 times 900 is 2,700 rupees a day. 30 times 2,700 is 81,000 rupees.
maths.context: When a well is polluted, a village must find water from somewhere else, and it costs money.
maths.why_maths: Working out the cost shows how big the price of pollution can be, long after the leak has stopped.

maths.problem: In an imagined pond, the oxygen readings were 8 milligrams per litre at 6 pm, 6 at 10 pm, 3 at 2 am and 2 at 6 am. Fish need at least 4. Between which two readings did the oxygen fall below 4? About when did it reach 4?
maths.answer: Between 10 pm and 2 am, at about 12:40 am.
maths.explain: At 10 pm it was 6 and at 2 am it was 3. It fell 3 in 4 hours, which is three quarters of a unit each hour. To fall from 6 to 4 takes 2 divided by three quarters, which is about 2 hours 40 minutes. 10 pm plus 2 hours 40 minutes is about 12:40 am.
maths.context: A pond with a lot of waste can run short of oxygen at night, when the algae use it and no sunlight makes more.
maths.why_maths: A line graph lets you find when a reading crosses a limit, even between two measurements.

maths.problem: In an oil spill test, 1 tablespoon of oil is 15 millilitres, and a bowl holds 300 millilitres of water. What fraction of the liquid in the bowl is oil, in its simplest form?
maths.explain: The total liquid is 300 plus 15, which is 315 millilitres. 15 out of 315 is the same as 1 out of 21, because 315 divided by 15 is 21.
maths.context: In the Oil Spill Race, each bowl holds 300 millilitres of water and 1 tablespoon of oil.
maths.why_maths: Writing the oil as a fraction shows that a small amount of oil can cover a whole bowl of water.

roots.context: We have thinned colour and scent into water, and followed dirty water into fish, rivers and sewage plants. Now we ask what this tells us about who is doing the checking, and about what 'away' really means.

deep_truth.truth: In the tumbler test, the colour vanished from the water after a few steps. The smell lasted one tumbler longer. So 'clean' is not only about the water, but also about who is checking and what they check with. Water that passes one check can fail another.
deep_truth.habit: We talk as if water were clean or dirty in itself, the way a stone is hard or soft. But 'clean' is a verdict that someone reaches with one check, such as looking, sniffing or reading a meter.
deep_truth.evidence: Your eyes lost the colour in a tumbler where your nose could still find the scent, and a chemist's instrument goes on finding things long after both give up. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your body is mostly water, and that water has been rain, river and cloud before it reached you. What goes into a river can come round to you.
three.what_is_life: Every living being checks water in their own way. A fish uses gills, a mayfly lives or dies by it, and a person uses eyes and nose. Living beings are some of the best water meters there are.
three.what_is_this_world: Water carries salt, soil, seeds and sewage from high places to low places. 'Away' only ever means somewhere else downstream.

roots.thread: A river looks like one thing, but it is water going round and round: sea, cloud, rain, river, sea. It carries the mountain's soil, the field's plant food, the town's sewage and the fish's bodies. Whatever one person puts in, a person further down drinks, and a fish further on keeps. The water is one water, and it shows up as every river, tank and tumbler. Clean and dirty are two ways that this one water meets different beings.

teachings.teaching: A hymn asks the Waters to carry away whatever is unclean in the speaker.
teachings.link: The hymn trusts water to carry things away. Science says that carrying away means carrying somewhere else, where someone else lives.

teachings.teaching: The highest good is like water. Water does good to all things and does not compete. She rests in the low places that others avoid.
teachings.link: Water settles in low places, so the lowest village on a river meets everything that all the villages above it put in.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water and bring the water back the next morning. The salt cannot be seen, but each sip from the top, middle and bottom tastes of salt.
teachings.link: In the tumbler test, the colour left the eyes but the scent stayed for the nose. Something unseen was still in every sip.

science.text: Matter is not made or lost when it mixes. Thinning something out spreads its atoms through more water, but every atom is still there.
Microplastics have been found in human blood. What they do to a body over a lifetime is not yet known.

other_view.view: 'Clean' has a plain meaning: below the safe limit for each named substance, set from health studies. That limit does not depend on who is checking. A look or a sniff is a poor guide, and the measurement is what counts.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet cooked or tested at home. Gone from Sight: the sums are worked out for a level teaspoon (5 millilitres) in 200 millilitres, so each tumbler is 41 times weaker. With 5 drops of food colour the tint should last to tumbler 2 and be gone by tumbler 3 or 4. A strong vanilla, rose or kewra essence should still be found by the nose in tumbler 3, and may be gone by tumbler 4. A weak or old essence may fade earlier, and the steps say what to do then. The die and the three cups are what keep the sniff test fair, and a child who gets all three right is unlikely to have guessed: 1 in 27. It needs at least 8 hours and a breezy place. The Oil Spill Race: the shine score is a judgement, and the paper-strip spot test is the fairer check. how_we_found_out.story: In the 1950s, in the fishing town of Minamata in Japan, cats began to stagger, spin and fall into the sea. Then people fell ill, with shaking hands, blurred sight and trouble walking. Neighbours feared it was catching and avoided the families. The Chisso chemical factory poured its waste into the bay. Like many people then, its managers believed the sea was so big that waste would thin out to nothing. In 1959 Dr Hajime Hosokawa, who worked at the factory's own hospital, fed the factory's waste water to a cat. The cat fell sick in the same way, and the company made him stop his tests. Researchers at Kumamoto University found the cause was mercury, in a form called methylmercury, which shellfish and fish had taken in and kept. It had built up in the bodies of the cats and people who ate them. The factory stopped the process in 1968, and the government named the waste as the cause. In 1969 the writer Michiko Ishimure told the patients' stories in a book.
how_we_found_out.who: Dr Hajime Hosokawa and researchers at Kumamoto University, with the writer Michiko Ishimure, who told the patients' stories
how_we_found_out.when: 1956 (the illness was reported), 1959 (the cat test and the mercury finding), 1968 (the cause was named), 1969 (Ishimure's book)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many believed the sea would thin the factory's waste to nothing, and that the illness was an infection. In fact the mercury did not thin out. Shellfish and fish took it in, kept it, and passed it up the food chain, so the fish held far more than the water around them.

quiz: Clear-looking water can still hold dissolved salt, chemicals or germs.
Dissolved things are too small to see, so only a test can show them.
The sea is so big that it can safely take any amount of waste.
Some wastes never break down, and they build up in mud and in animals.
Pouring dye into more water makes it weaker, but the same amount of dye is there.
Dilution spreads a substance thinner, so the strength falls but the amount stays.
Boiling makes any water safe, even if it has chemicals like arsenic.
Boiling kills germs, but chemicals stay behind and get stronger as the water boils away.
Waste that microbes can eat can still kill fish by using up oxygen in the water.
Microbes multiply on the waste and use the oxygen dissolved in water that fish breathe.
Lead and mercury are eaten by microbes and turn harmless in time.
Elements cannot be broken down by anyone; they can only move or be locked away.
A pollutant can grow stronger at each step up a food chain.
Animals at the top eat many contaminated animals, so they carry far more than the water does.
An algal bloom happens when water has too little plant food.
Too much nitrogen and phosphorus feeds algae until they form a thick green crowd.
A sewage treatment plant removes most dissolved chemicals from factories.
It removes solids, microbe food and germs, but few dissolved chemicals.
Oil spreads in a thin layer on water because it is lighter and does not mix.
Oil floats on top, so it can be held in by a barrier, skimmed or soaked up.
odd: Microbes can eat the first three and break them down; lead is an element nothing can break down.
A cloth can catch the first three bits, but salt is dissolved into pieces too small for any cloth.
The first three enter water at one place; runoff arrives from the whole land at once.
The first three take oil out of the water; a dispersant breaks it into droplets that stay in the water.
The first three add nutrients that can feed an algal bloom; clean spring water adds none.
